history.title: Home [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: A fun adventure for little kids....not so much for adults
history.text: When a bunch of my co-workers raved about having seen and loved this movie, I knew I had to give it a look. Add to the fact that Jim Parsons of the Big Bang Theory was the voice of one of the lead characters, and I was all set to have a fun time. And while I DID sort of like it, it's not without its problems. On the run from their enemy, the planet-destroying Gorg, the alien Boov find Earth suitable for a place to call "home". Led by Captain Smek, they commence their "friendly" invasion of the planet, relocating the humans, whom the Boov deem as simple and backwards, to other parts of the planet, while the Boov inhabit their homes in a quick and bloodless conquest. One of the Boov, named Oh, is a more excited, freethinking member of the species, who decides to invite the Boov to his apartment for a housewarming party, despite everyone not liking him. Meanwhile, a preteen girl named Tip drives through her home city to find her mother, after being separated from her during the invasion, leaving her with just her cat. But when Oh accidentally e-mails his party invitation to the Gorg and alerts the enemy to the Boov's presence, he's labeled a menace to society and becomes a fugitive. He soon accidentally runs into Tip, and from there, the two misfits must team up to not only find Tip's mother, but fix Oh's mistake and save the world...and in the process, learn more about one another and close the gap between their very different cultures. Getting the good out of the way, both Tip and Oh are very likeable. Both Rihanna and Jim Parsons were perfectly cast as the smart and adventurous girl and quirky, loveable alien. Both of them face being outcasts from their respective societies, and through the course of their adventure, they learn how to find similarities in their cultures, while also respecting one another's differences. Oh, and by extension, the Boov, especially go through alot of character growth; learning that humans are much more smart and complicated than they once believed, and that simply running away from their problems all the time won't solve anything. There's also a twist involving both the Boov and Gorg leaders that definitely teaches to not judge a book by its cover. The big problem with all this, however, lies in the execution. I have a feeling this was a movie that was made specifically for a younger audience in mind, because there's little to no subtlety in this. From the Boov changing color to suit their emotions, to the characters just saying outright how they feel, practically everything is spelt out for the audience. Any and all possible twists, you can see coming from a mile away. And while I got a few laughs and chuckles here and there, most of the jokes focused on how babyish the Boov are, and after a while, it got tiring. Not to mention the film is almost non-stop talking, with very little slow, quiet moments to let anything sink in. And the few slow moments there are, it's filled with songs. Which, speaking of, nearly every ten minutes, another Rihanna song would pop up to fill, what otherwise would've been, a quiet/instrumental moment. I have nothing against Rihanna (in fact, I love her music), but while the songs were really catchy, they didn't really add anything to the plot, and in many spots, could've been removed. There's also an (admittedly) amazing sequence that happens in Paris, ending with the Eiffel Tower being flipped upside down....a sequence that, in my opinion, should've been saved for the film's finale, rather than be in the middle. The actual finale is kind of weak by comparison. SPOILER ALERT On a related note, we eventually find out that the Gorg isn't all that evil, and all he wanted was an item that the Boov possessed, which was important to the Gorg species. Well that's all fine and good, except....the Gorg STILL destroyed entire planets beforehand, so....once they get their item back, everything is just fine and dandy? For a movie that's supposed to be promoting "love and tolerance", that's kind of a dark skeleton in the closet you left hanging, guys.... END OF SPOILER Considering Dreamworks' past output, like "How to Train Your Dragon", "Kung Fu Panda", and "Rise of the Guardians", I guess I got spoiled. Even in their more comedy-based movies, like "Shrek" and the "Madagasgar" films, their jokes at least had a bit of an older/adult edge to them. Here, the jokes are definitely for the ten and under crowd. Not that that's bad. It's just...I guess I was going in, expecting one thing, and got something else. At least I now know why so many of my co-workers raved about this movie...because all of said co-workers have little kids. And ultimately, I think that's what this film is best for....little kids. The aliens act like kids, and the audience is talked to as if they're kids. And it's a shame, because I can sense a really great movie in here, somewhere...it's just that the non-subtlety keeps it at just the "good/okay" level. Bottom line, I'm glad I saw it, but I'll probably not watch it again. It's cute....that's all the more I can really say...it's cute. If you have kids, then by all means, give this a go. It just wasn't my cup of tea. If you're a pre-teen to teenager/young adult, and want your animated comedy with a bit more of an edge, watch "Shrek". Or if you want a more gripping adventure, watch "Rise of the Guardians".

history.title: Jack And The Cuckoo-Clock Heart [DVD]
history.review_title: A strange movie that's more creepy and confusing than entertaining
history.text: It was through this studio's earlier film, "A Monster in Paris", as well as some word of mouth, that I came across this odd looking little movie. Although my tastes lean more towards science fiction, I'm always up for a good fairy tale, and after LOVING "A Monster in Paris", I figured another outing with the same French studio would be just as good. Sadly, this wasn't to be the case, for this is, no doubt, one of the strangest and trippiest movies I've watched in a long time (and not in the good way). In Edinburgh, Scotland 1874, a boy named Jack is born on the coldest day ever. Due to the extreme cold, he's born with a frozen heart which will not beat. The attendant midwife Madeleine saves his life by replacing his heart with a cuckoo clock. She then advises him of three rules to prevent his untimely death; he must never play with the hands of the clock, he must never lose his temper, and finally, he must never fall in love. But upon Jack's first journey into town, he becomes infatuated with a girl named Miss Acacia, as well as runs afowl of a bully named Joe, who's also in love with her. When a confrontation with Joe forces Jack to leave town, he then goes on a quest to be reunited with Miss Acacia. And along the way, he learns both the good and the dangers of falling in love. Will he find a way to love Acacia without being hurt? Or will he find romance at the cost of his life? If you follow my other reviews here on Amazon, then you might find me echoing a similar thing I said in my review of the book, "The Night Circus"--that this movie, to me, seems like the creators got so wrapped up in the world building and artwork that the characters and story suffered as a consequence. This film is certainly pretty to look at, especially if you're a fan of the steampunk genre...and that's about it. But the characters themselves straddle the line of the Uncanny Valley. Unlike "A Monster in Paris", which had highly stylized characters similar to a Pixar movie, this film took a slightly more realistic route...and in doing so, all the humans look and move like dolls with dead eyes, and they barely make any sort of expressions no matter what emotion they're supposed to be feeling; making the whole movie creepy to watch at times. And sadly, the characters don't make things much better. They're all enormously flat and boring. Jack seems to have no other motivations or hopes or dreams beyond chasing this one girl he likes. And speaking of Acacia, she's just as bland, with her and Jack falling in love literally at first sight without knowing a single thing about each other. Granted, they interact a bit later on once they find each other again, but it's not enough for me to buy their relationship. And Joe is the biggest mystery; having no personality beyond just being a jerk and a bully. It's like he was added in just for the sake of having a villain, which I don't think this movie really needed. Honestly, the best character was the traveling magician that Jack runs into along his journey, making me wish HE was the main character instead. (And on a side note, I think the English voice cast wasn't the greatest. They do a decent job in terms of acting, but the voices for Jack and Acacia, especially when they're supposed to be little kids, are WAY too deep. Ten year old Jack sounds like he's 20, and young Acacia sounds like a grown woman.) As for the plot, it's a fairly decent one on paper, and clever too--about how a boy learns the meaning of true love, and the girl literally holding the key to his heart. But the presentation of said idea just makes it utterly confusing. They play up Jack's cuckoo clock heart like he's some weird anomaly...but then we see people with homemade artificial limbs, a man with a xylophone for a spine, and circus folk with two heads, or big heads, or literal fairies flying around. And Acacia, meanwhile, sprouts thorns around her neck when she's distressed (and no, we never get an explanation), and randomly floats in the air when she's happy. So clearly, this is a magical, fantasy/fairy tale world....which makes it much harder to see Jack as such an outcast. It would've made more sense if this were like "Edward Scissorhands", where the rest of the world is 'normal', and Jack is the only unique one of his kind. But when your entire world is filled with strange people, it makes his struggle that much harder to accept. On a final note, this is probably the weirdest music choices I've ever heard in a movie. The steampunk style this movie is set in would make you think that a classical score would be the order of the day...but instead, scenes are filled with rock and roll cues, as well as some hip-hop beats, and the songs that the characters sing are not only forgettable, but constantly come out of left field with barely any segway into them. Half the time, they don't even rhyme. Joe doesn't even get a song. Instead, he has two moments where he randomly starts spouting poetry that...well, he isn't quite talking, but he's not fully singing either. Pick one or the other, people... Maybe this movie is just too 'avant-garde' for me, but as it stands, between the weird visuals, the bland characters, the so-so animation on the humans, the random songs, and the odd music choices, this whole film is nothing but an artsy mess. For those of you who like Tim Burton's output, or surrealness and steampunk, then maybe you'll like this. But for me, I'm sticking with "A Monster in Paris". At least that was a fairy tale I could clearly follow and understand.

history.title: Kingsman 2: The Golden Circle
history.review_title: The love letter to classic spy films gets a worthy sequel
history.text: Being a lover of James Bond, The Man from UNCLE, and plenty of other spy shows and movies, I was really intrigued to see the first Kingsman film when it came out in theaters, but unfortunately, wasn't able to see it until it hit DVD. And after thoroughly enjoying it, I vowed to make up for my previous mistake and made the trek to theaters to see the highly anticipated sequel. The result was a wild ride that was just as good as the previous installment, with more than its fair share of shocking twists, great action, and hilarious moments. A year has passed since Eggsy and the secret organization, Kingsman, saved the world from Richmond Valentine's neurological wave broadcast. He has since taken his late mentor Harry Hart's title of Galahad and lives with Crown Princess Tilde of Sweden. On his way home, he's ambushed by a former Kingsman trainee who lost his arm and vocal cords during the Valentine incident. Eggsy manages to escape in a car chase across London, but the agent's severed cybernetic arm hacks into the Kingsman servers through the car's computer system, and, by giving the info to his boss, all of Kingsman's outposts are subsequently destroyed. With very little resources at their disposal, Eggsy and the few remaining Kingsman agents follow the Doomsday protocol, which leads them to Statesman, a secret American organization posing as a Bourbon whiskey distillery in Kentucky. From there, the two mirroring agencies team up to take down the organization responsible for the Kingsman's destruction---"The Golden Circle". I'll do my best to leave a proper review, but bear in mind that there's plenty of plot points that I can't really talk about without major spoilers, as the movie sends the viewer on plenty of twists and turns---some for the hilarious--others for the horrifying, as plenty of major characters from the previous film get the axe fairly early on. This, I believe, is mostly to make way for a slew of brand new characters from the Statesman division---all of whom are equipped with their own brand of wild west themed gadgetry. But Eggsy still gets plenty of development, as he tries his best to make his former mentor proud, and balance his secret agent life with his love life. As for the villain, our main antagonist this time around is Poppy Adams---a sweet spoken, but megalomaniacal lady who runs The Golden Circle; her plans involving lacing every recreational drug available with a deadly toxin, then holding the thousands affected hostage---agreeing to give over the antidote if the U.S. President gives in to her demands. While I feel that the previous film's villain was just a bit more interesting, Poppy is just as memorable with her robotic servants, outlandish hideout, and holding Elton John hostage (who plays himself and arguably gets some of the funniest moments of the movie). And much like the first film, her schemes also lead to a heavy question of morality. Should any of the affected victims really be saved, or is killing people who experiment with drugs actually doing the world a favor? As for the action scenes, they're well done, and although EXTREMELY violent and bloody, they're choreographed well enough that you can easily tell what's going on and smoothly follow the action. (So many action movies now have the fights go by so quick, it can be hard to tell what's going on when it all becomes a blur.) The cinematography and choreography blends seamlessly, allowing the stunt work to be cranked up to eleven. And though many of the fights and set pieces can get outright ridiculous, that's kind of the point. This is a film that operates completely on the "rule of cool". It knows exactly what it is, and completely revels in throwing realism out the window in favor of giving the audience what they really want. But more than anything, this film serves as a loving homage and tribute to classic spy movies (specifically ones from the 60s), while also keeping things fresh and updated. It seems that now a days, spy movies have gone the Jason Bourne route, and want to be more gritty and "realistic" (even James Bond seems to be heading down this path). So it was nice to see a film that gives the spy genre a swift kick in the pants, and just be FUN again. Bottom line, if you love spy films and shows like classic Bond, the Avengers, In Like Flint (etc.), this is the movie for you. It's just as good as the first, and it leaves me wanting yet another sequel.

history.title: Daredevil: The Complete First Season
history.review_title: An exciting, well written series about the Man Without Fear
history.text: I've long been a loyal follower of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, enjoying nearly all of the films and the continuing story they've been weaving for almost ten years now. But starting with "Agents of SHIELD", the MCU has been branching out to television as well. And while the films have been pretty much one mega hit after another, the TV side of the spectrum has been more of a mixed bag. I've heard great things about "Agent Carter", while "SHIELD" seems to have fallen in the camp of "you either like it or you don't", and the recent "Inhumans" has yet to receive any positive review (that I could find, anyway). Plus, a movie is much easier to get through, while a TV show is more of a commitment, and with so many branching shows now, I was kind of turned off to seeing any of them, though thankfully, you don't have to watch any of the shows to understand the movies---the shows are great companion pieces to the MCU, but the show runners have wisely kept them fairly separate from the films. But then the MCU dared to try something different. They wanted to bring their more "darker" characters to the screen, but rather than tone down the violence for the general viewing audience, they instead decided to launch their series on video streaming sites, where the censorship would be more lax. For this new movement, the superhero they chose to be their flagship character was Daredevil---one of Marvel's more underrated, but still interesting heroes that I knew a fair amount about, and was interested to see the MCU's take on him. And though the show's been out for quite a while as of the time of this review, I was finally able to make the time to sit down and give all 13 episodes a watch. And what I came away with was nothing short of amazing. The series tells the tale of Matt Murdock--a defense attorney who, as a child, was blinded in an accident after saving a man from being hit by a truck carrying hazardous chemicals, resulting in his remaining senses being heightened to superhuman levels. Armed with just his super senses, his wits, and his fists, he upholds the criminal justice system by day, but then puts on a mask and unleashes vigilante justice by night when the law isn't enough. His nightly excursions soon catch the attention of every crime syndicate in and around his neighborhood...including the mysterious, power hungry businessman leading them all, Wilson Fisk--aka, The Kingpin. Will Matt be able to become the hero that Hell's Kitchen needs? Or will the very city he's trying to protect be caught in the crossfire of this crime war and go up in smoke? Despite working with a television budget, the production values of this show are very high, and oftentimes, it's easy to forget that you're watching a small screen show, and not just a super long movie. Though probably a great deal of it is helped by the fact that Daredevil is a "street level" superhero, so anyone expecting grandiose, epic level battles ala "Ironman" or "Doctor Strange" is going to be disappointed. This is a show that relies heavily on tight scripting and character development, resulting in a series that's half court room drama--half crime boss/political thriller....with a blind, superhuman ninja thrown in. Not a single episode is boring, or used for filler. Every episode serves to further the story, and though Matt doesn't get his famous costume until the last episode, his journey getting there is well worth it. Things move along at a steady pace, and the plots always keep the viewer guessing, with constant call backs to past episodes. Characters or details that seem inconsequential at first often times turn out to be incredibly important later on, and sharp eyed viewers will be greatly rewarded for paying attention. But the series' greatest strength lies in its characters and clever writing. From the word go, you understand why Matt is the kind of person he is, and why he would turn to taking up a mask to do what he believes is the right thing. He's incredibly kind and charming, and seeks to help out the little guy and other less fortunate people who's problems are often ignored. But he's far from perfect, and everything he does, both good and bad, has serious consequences. Luckily, he makes his share of unlikely allies, from his church's priest (who tries to help keep him on a righteous path), to honest cop Brett Mahoney, to the sympathetic nurse, Claire (who's constantly patching him up), to the hard-nosed reporter Ben Ulrich (who will do whatever it takes to get a story), to his secretary Karen (who clearly has some sort of tragic past of her own). But by and large, his greatest friend is Foggy Nelson; his roommate since college and big hearted law partner, who never dances around Matt's disability, and always has his back when things turn sour. And as for the villains, they're just as interesting and multi layered---most notably Wilson Fisk, who acts almost as a dark mirror to Matt's heroism. He has his own twisted sense of morality and justice, and will go to any length to "clean up" the city, even if his method is by way of the mafia--using fear and manipulation to secretly take control of both the police and the media. Both hero and villain have similar sad pasts, with their dialogue often carrying deeper meanings that can also be applied to their respective opposite. And when crap hits the fan, it hits it hard, with plenty of recurring characters meeting sudden, shocking ends that I didn't see coming. And perhaps that's the point and the series' theme---in a world where it's unclear who can be trusted, one can't rely on just what they see. It takes all your senses and using your head to weed out evil. At times brutal, but also exciting, this is a well thought out and brilliantly crafted superhero thriller that dares to show the unseen, ugly side of the MCU, and proves that the things happening down on the streets are just as interesting and important as the cosmic adventures we normally see on the big screen. I now can't wait to dive into Season 2, as well as check out its companion series, "Jessica Jones".

history.title: Batman vs. Two-Face (Blu-ray/DVD/Digital)
history.review_title: A perfect swan song for Adam West and one last salute to the legendary TV show
history.text: Ever since his debut in the 30s, Batman has been one of the most popular and infamous superheroes ever created. Much of his success lies in his character's versatility. At some turns, he can be dark, grim, and gritty, and at other turns, lighthearted and funny. Every reinvention and reinterpretation is perfectly valid, and has gained fans across generations. But the one version that's arguably become the most famous of all is the colorful and campy take from the 1960's staring Adam West and Burt Ward as the Dynamic Duo. While some may laugh at its inherent hokey-ness, for certain generations, this was the version of Batman they grew up with and came to love. And even today, thanks to reruns, it continues to be a well loved show by a new age of fans (younger kids especially). And after the success of the first animated movie, "Return of the Caped Crusaders", my parents and I were really excited when this sequel was announced. And I'm happy to report that this movie is the perfect way to dip into that nostalgia again, and is even BETTER than the previous film. At the height of the groovy 60s, Batman and Robin are on the case when Dr. Hugo Strange develops a machine to remove the inherent evilness in Gotham's most sinister villains. Joining the Dynamic Duo at the presentation is Bruce Wayne's old friend, district attorney Harvey Dent. But when a horrible accident causes the machine to malfunction, the resulting explosion scars half of Harvey's face and infects him with the siphoned evil energy from the villains, transforming him into the deadly Two-Face. Bruce Wayne stops at nothing to help rehabilitate his old friend, and in time, Harvey is eventually cured of his duality. But when a string of robberies break out around the city, Batman must use all his skills and wit to solve the crime, while also not letting his friendship with Harvey cloud his judgment. Has Harvey Dent regressed into becoming Two-Face again? Or is the district attorney being framed? Starting with the acting, Adam West, Burt Ward, and Julie Newmar all come back to lend their voices to their respective characters, and their delivery is spot on as if they never left the show. And since most, if not all, of the rest of the cast has sadly passed away, the new voice actors all do a great job of emulating Cesar Romero, Burgess Meredith, and the like. (Commissioner Gordon's the only one that sounds more than a bit off to me. That, and Burt Ward's voice definitely shows his age a bit, but now I'm just being nitpicky.) And the animation and art direction is fantastic, with character models that look just like the actors and a color pallet that gives off the old show's vibes, without being TOO over the top. As for the story, it plays out just like an extended episode of the show, complete with the theme music, bat fights, Bat-tusi, and every BIFF!, BAM! and POW! intact. And because it's animated, the writers and artists were able to add more details the live series wasn't able to do, such as showing how the batpole costume changer actually works, a few new vehicles like the Bat-shuttle, and some new areas of the Batcave, like the infamous trophy room from the comics. Clearly, the team behind this movie had a lot of love and respect for the 60s series, and wanted to do it the proper justice. And William Shatner does an impressive job as Two-Face (and Harvey's even drawn to look a bit like Shatner). Although the movie keeps in the lighthearted spirit of the show, it also dares to take the material just a bit more seriously, with Bruce having to grapple with the fact that his best friend has turned villianous. And Two-Face's theme of duality seeps into the other characters as well, with the Dynamic Duo getting in a heated argument over how to handle Dent---a fight that very nearly ends their partnership. And it all leads up to a final, climatic fight that....well, I won't spoil it, but considering this was Adam West's final performance before passing away, it's serves as a perfect end to such a legendary show. So to any and all fans of the colorful TV show, you NEED to give this movie a watch, as it's not only a great follow up to the previous animated film, but is also a great send off to Adam West and the legacy he left behind.

history.review_title: Ragnarok and roll with the best of the Thor films
history.text: I've long been a loyal follower of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, enjoying nearly all of the films and the continuing story they've been weaving for over ten years now. But it seems that out of all their main characters, Thor always gets the short end of the stick. His first movie was perfectly fine, while the sequel, "The Dark World", has been heralded by most fans as one of the weakest/worst movies of all the MCU films (and I kind of tend to agree--it wasn't awful, but certainly forgettable). So when a third installment was announced, the response was initially lukewarm. But as more trailers were unveiled, I got more and more excited, knowing that whatever we were going to get looked FAR better than Thor's previous two outings. And my prediction was right. This is not only Thor's best movie, but easily one of the most entertaining of all the MCU films. Two years after the events of "Age of Ultron", Thor has been unsuccessfully searching for the Infinity Stones, and is imprisoned by the fire demon, Surtur. Surtur reveals that Thor's father, Odin, is no longer on Asgard, and that the realm will soon be destroyed in the prophesied end-of-days, Ragnarök. After defeating Surtur, Thor returns to Asgard to find his brother Loki posing as Odin. Thor forces Loki to help him find their father, and with some help from Doctor Strange, they locate Odin in Norway. Odin then reveals that he's dying, and that his passing will allow his firstborn child, the goddess of death, Hela, to escape from a prison she was sealed in long ago. With Odin's passing, Hela is freed, and she subsequently destroys Thor's hammer Mjolnir, then forces him and Loki out into space to die. But while she sets out to conquer Asgard, unbeknownst to her, Thor and Loki fall through a wormhole and crash land on Sakaar--a garbage planet where they're both captured, and where Thor is taken to serve as a gladiator for the planet's ruler, the Grandmaster. But after discovering his old friend, the Hulk, has also been living on the planet for some time, along with a long lost fellow Asguardian, Thor rallies together his friends and the planet's citizens to overthrow the Grandmaster and find a way off the planet, so that he may return home, defeat Hela, and save Asgard. Anyone who's become bored of Thor's character in his previous two films will be pleasantly surprised here. Gone is the traditional Shakespearian talk, and what we get instead is a fast paced, funny movie that dials the humor up to 11 and, dare I say it, is even funnier than the Guardians of the Galaxy films. Even for a situation as serious as Asgard potentially being destroyed (and with plenty of previously established Asgardians meeting their ends), the movie hits the perfect balance of knowing when to be serious, and when to let the humor and absurdness of certain situations shine. (And to any Led Zeppelin fans, yes, the "Immigrant Song" from the trailers is in the movie, and used to great effect.) About the only criticism I can give is that the plot is incredibly fast paced, particularly towards the start, where a TON of info-dumping is given to explain what happened between "The Dark World" and now, and give backstory to the new characters---thus revealing that many of the previously established lore from the past Thor movies either was a lie, or a cover up. But it's all handled very well and makes total sense (it just goes by fast, so be prepared to pay close attention). Every single character gets their time to shine, and not one person steals the whole movie. Everyone, both hero and villain, is funny and memorable. Hela is having the time of her life destroying everything in her wake; Asgardian newcomer Valkerie has an interesting past (and though as much as I like Jane Foster, Val arguably makes for a better love interest for Thor), and the Hulk finally gets a chance to fully talk and articulate himself, thus leading to the movie not only being about Thor, but also being a small, sly adaption of the famous "Planet Hulk" storyline from the comics. And it all ends with a shocking final battle that does for Thor what "The Winter Soldier" did to Captain America. So to any naysayers of the Thor films, this third installment will definitely be your cup of tea. With a fast, engaging plot, memorable characters, and witty humor, this is the huge kick in the pants that Thor needed.

history.review_title: DC's greatest heroes unite....for a very mixed bag adventure
history.text: While Marvel Studios seems to have been on a role for the past few years, churning out one superhero hit after the next, DC has had to play massive catch up. It seems they've fallen into a rut of having all their movies revolve around either Superman or Batman, with all the other members of the Justice League getting pushed to the wayside (being confined to just having television series). So after the huge success of Wonder Woman's solo film, and the foreshadowing that was dropped in "Batman v Superman", fans, including me, were hyped to finally see the most famous superhero team put to screen. Would this movie get DC caught up to Marvel? Or will they continue to succeed just on TV, leaving their rival to dominate the silver screen? The end result is a bit of a mixed bag. On the one hand, the film is way too short and disjointed. But on the other hand, it delivers a great many things that comic fans have been longing to see put to screen. Thousands of years ago, an alien entity known as Steppenwolf, and his army of Parademons from the planet Apocalypse, attempted to conquer and remake Earth through the combined energies of a trio of powerful artifacts known as the Mother Boxes. But he was foiled by a unified army that included the Olympian Gods, Amazons, Atlanteans, humans, and Green Lanterns. After repelling Steppenwolf's army, the Mother Boxes were separated and hidden in locations around the world. Cut to the present day, and the world is in mourning after the death of Superman (after the events of "BvS"). This triggers the Mother Boxes to reactivate, and Steppenwolf returns to Earth in an effort to regain favor with his master, Darkseid. With the fate of the world at stake, Batman and Wonder Woman team up to face this new threat, while also calling in three new heroes to help: the king of Atlantis, Aquaman--half man/half robotic super genius, Cyborg---and the scientific, super speedster, the Flash. Together, this quintet of superheroes must put aside their differences and band together before the world is transformed into a Hell-on-Earth. There's one part of this plot that I can't really talk about without spoiling anything, in regards to a certain character, so : SPOILERS BELOW By far, this movie's greatest asset is its characters. Despite the obvious bickering here and there towards the start, the whole team meshes together really well. Everyone has something to do and a role to play, and by the end, everyone's either become a stronger fighter, or have learned to come out of their shells a bit and make themselves known to the public. Batman has since learned his lesson from "BvS" and is generally more of a team player, while Wonder Woman is still, in a way, grieving over the death of Steve Trevor, and is on the fence about coming out of hiding. Cyborg, being half computer, serves as the tech expert, and is a bit more logical and reserved, but his friendship with the team helps him regain his humanity. And though Aquaman is a bit under-utilized, his observations and snarky comments are on point. But far and away the most entertaining of the bunch is the Flash, who is still coming into his own, but excited to save the world, and is constantly cracking jokes (but does know when to be serious). And as a consequence, his friendly teasing, as well as the team camaraderie, makes the film as a whole ten times more lighthearted and fun compared to the previous films in the DC universe. However, the film DOES have its share of problems. Firstly, Steppenwolf is a totally forgettable villain, with no real motivation beyond just wanting to take over the world and drop hints towards the eventual arrival of Darkseid. But this could also be due to the film's other major problem---the pacing. I find it a bit ironic that in my "BvS" review, I criticized the enormous run time, because here, we got the opposite problem. The movie is INCREDIBLY rushed. The origin stories of the new characters, as well as the plot, is given in quick info dumps in order to try and fit everything in, and as a consequence, moments that should have a bigger emotional impact are just glossed over. The worst is when Superman is brought back to life. His big return is met with little fan fare, and feels more like just a tacked on afterthought that doesn't have as big an impact as it should have. Clark gets over it fairly quickly and acts like he just took a quick nap instead of coming back from the dead. So as it stands, the film is a hard, halfway split. The action and set pieces are great, and the characters and their interactions are great, but the story definitely needed more time to develop and perhaps at least just one more movie to build up to it (the Marvel movie formula has been working for a reason after all). Not that it isn't interesting, but it definitely could've used some better editing and a longer run time. But the stuff that's good is really good, and for what it's worth, I enjoyed it. Here's hoping that we'll see more of the League in future films, as the stuff they teased throughout sounds very promising.

history.title: Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind (Bluray/DVD Combo) [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: An anti-war / save the environment film with outstanding animation and visuals
history.text: Anyone who is a fan and lover of animation has (and should) seen at least one film by Studio Ghibli, and its acclaimed writer and director, Hayao Miyazaki. His beautiful and stunning movies are known the world over, and has inspired artists everywhere. But although I've grown up with many of his films, there ARE still a few I have yet to see for various reasons. And I'm embarrassed to say this was one of them. For how famous this film is, it's only now that I'm finally watching it. And the journey I was taken on was nothing short of breathtaking and introspective. One thousand years have passed since the Seven Days of Fire, an apocalyptic war that destroyed civilization and created the vast Toxic Jungle, a poisonous forest swarming with giant mutant insects. In the kingdom of the Valley of the Wind, Nausicaä, the princess, explores the jungle and communicates with its creatures, including the gigantic, insect-like armored Ohm. She hopes to understand the jungle and find a way for it and humans to co-exist. But one night, a cargo aircraft from the kingdom of Tolmekia crashes in the Valley. Its sole passenger, Princess Lastelle of Pejite, pleads with Nausicaä to destroy the cargo and dies. The cargo is an embryo of a Giant Warrior, one of the lethal humanoid bio-weapons that caused the Seven Days of Fire. Tolmekia, a military state, seized the embryo and Lastelle from Pejite, but their plane was attacked by mutant insects and crashed. The next morning, Tolmekian troops, led by Princess Kushana, invade the Valley of the Wind, kill Nausicaä's father and capture the embryo, with Kushana planning to mature the Giant Warrior and use it to burn the Toxic Jungle. But Nausicaa knows there's more to the Jungle and its inhabitants than what meets the eye, and with the help of the friends she makes along the way from each of the three kingdoms, it's up to her to make everyone understand that humanity will have to somehow make peace with nature if they're to survive. The visuals and animation, as per usual in a Miyazaki film, are utterly breathtaking to look at and watch. The amount of sheer detail put into every background and character movement is incredible, and the various magical creatures are imaginative and unlike anything you've ever seen before in a fairy tale, from giant insects to fantastic flying machines. All the characters are well developed and/or three dimensional, mainly Nausicaa herself, who can be reasonably afraid of certain danger, but is extremely brave and resourceful, and uses her knowledge of nature to help the rest of humanity understand just how much they've abused the environment. She believes in the value of life regardless of its form, and through her actions, stops a war. The English dub voice cast also does a fantastic job. Most, if not all the actors, fall into their roles perfectly. The only hang up I have is with Patrick Stewart. He IS a phenomenal actor, and his voice work is fantastic....but his voice is just so recognizable, it can get just a teeny bit distracting (but that's my own problem, not the movie's fault). About the only real negative I can give is the choice of music. I'm not sure if the version I watched was all the original Japanese soundtrack, or if some of the music was swapped out for an Americanized version (as some dubs are wont to do), but in any case, there's more than a couple action sequences that utilize these weird techno tracks that instantly date the movie for me. Rather than anything orchestral, it sounds like it came out of a 1980s arcade game. Still, I'm glad I finally gave this movie a watch, as it carries fantastic environmental messages that don't beat you over the head. If you're interested in Miyazaki's work, then definitely check it out.

history.title: Princess Mononoke (Bluray/DVD Combo) [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: A complicated battle between man and nature with stunning animation but a mixed bag of characters
history.text: Anyone who is a fan and lover of animation has (and should) seen at least one film by Studio Ghibli, and its acclaimed writer and director, Hayao Miyazaki. His beautiful and stunning movies are known the world over, and has inspired artists everywhere. But although I've grown up with many of his films, there ARE still a few I have yet to see for various reasons. And I'm embarrassed to say this was one of them. For how famous this film is, it's only now that I'm finally watching it. And though the journey I was taken on was nothing short of breathtaking, it's not without its problems. In ancient Japan, a young warrior prince named Ashitaka is inflicted with a deadly curse while fighting off a demon attacking his village. Forced to leave his home, he heads west in search of the Great Forest Spirit, who he hopes can cure him. There, he stumbles into a bitter conflict between Lady Eboshi, who has been systematically destroying the forest and killing its magical creatures to build her town, and the enigmatic Princess Mononoke, a young girl raised by wolves, who will stop at nothing to prevent the humans from destroying her home, and the forest spirits and animal gods who live there. Now caught in the middle of this fight, Ashitaka must find a peaceful solution to the conflict, or else his curse will slowly consume and kill him. The visuals and animation, as per usual in a Miyazaki film, are utterly breathtaking to look at and watch. The amount of sheer detail put into every background and character movement is incredible, and the various magical creatures are imaginative and unlike anything you've ever seen before in a fairy tale. Even stronger is its environmental messages, and the conflict between humankind's growth and development and nature's need for preservation. Neither side of the issue is completely in the right or wrong, and both the humans, animals, and nature gods are all fighting for their fair share of the world---that good and evil and violence and peace exist in all of us, and it's all about finding a balance. My main problem, however, lies in the characters. Arguably, the best, most interesting character in the film is Lady Eboshi--the leader of Irontown who is tough, but fair to her people, and is the perfect example of a "likeable villain". Her village is a refuge for social outcasts, including former brothel workers and lepers, whom Eboshi employs to manufacture firearms to defend against the gods. As such, she's well respected by her people, making her not so much evil as just extremely misguided, due to her attempts to destroy the magical creatures that upset her town's progress at every turn. The other two protagonists, on the other hand, don't fare as well by comparison. Ashitaka's demon curse helps make him realize that hate and killing isn't the answer to solving the conflict between man and nature, but...it doesn't seem to really hinder him all that much. I was completely expecting him to turn into a full on monster at some point, but instead, he just has one or two close calls and that's about it. Honestly, there were a few times I actually forgot he was even infected with a curse at all. But my biggest sticking point is Mononoke herself (or San as she's actually called). It's weird that the movie is named after her, when she's actually not in it all that much and doesn't really do too much in the grand scheme of the film. You'd think with her being a human raised by wolves that SHE would be the perfect choice of main character to have to be the one to unite humans and nature, but....nope. She just spends the majority of the time complaining about the evils of humanity while Ashitaka gets most of the screen time. While I AM glad I finally saw this, it's definitely not my most favorite of Miyazaki's work. If you want to watch a Studio Ghibli film with a more emotional and likeable main character, and an environmental message that's executed a bit simpler, then go watch "Nausicca of the Valley of the Wind."

history.review_title: The "Empire Strikes Back" of the new sequel trilogy
history.text: Star Wars...two words that've become a household name, right up there with Indiana Jones and Jurassic Park. Love it or hate it, the original trilogy of films are classics that stunned audiences around the world with its stellar special effects and sci-fi mythos; becoming a mainstay for an entire generation. But after a trilogy of lackluster prequels, the prospect of a trilogy of new films taking place years after "Return of the Jedi", with an entirely different cast of characters, made me cautiously optimistic. But after "The Force Awakens" exceeded my expectations, I eagerly dove into this next installment to see what would become of our new cast of heroes and villains. In the end, like many of the fans, I'm left a bit divided. While some moments and elements greatly expanded and improved upon the previous film, there were other points that just left me scratching my head. (I'll do my best to explain while spoiling as little as possible.) Approximately 30 years after the destruction of the second Death Star, Luke Skywalker, the supposed last Jedi, has disappeared. The First Order has risen from the remains of the fallen Galactic Empire, and seeks to eliminate Luke and the Republic. The Resistance, backed by the Republic, and led by Luke's sister, Princess Leia, opposes them while searching for Luke to enlist his aid. Picking up immediately after the events of "The Force Awakens", the Resistance fighters are on the run from the First Order, with many of the rebels divided over what's the best course of action to take, including pilot Poe Dameron, who enlists Finn, BB-8, and a mechanic named Rose, to embark on their own, secret plan to take down the fleet chasing them. Meanwhile, Rey has located Luke Skywalker, who has become a recluse after his old student, Kylo Ren, betrayed and destroyed Luke's emerging Jedi order. But Rey is convinced that Kylo can somehow be redeemed, while Kylo is insistent on turning Rey to the Dark Side. And when these forces of Light and Dark finally clash, their confrontation could spell either a new hope or complete disaster for the galaxy. One of the film's strongest assets is some of the new ideas it brings to the Star Wars mythos, with some new abilities being done with the Force, as well as a plethora of plot twists and turns that I didn't see coming. Just when I thought I had the plot figured out, the writing would throw another curveball that continued to surprise me all the way through to the end. There's also some great callbacks to previous movies in the saga, and while this film has some parallels to "The Empire Strikes Back", the comparisons aren't nearly as heavy handed as they were between "New Hope/Force Awakens". The rest of the movie, however, is a bit of a mixed bag. The worst, for me, is the secret mission that Finn and Rose embark on. Without spoilers, it's a sequence/sub-plot that either should've been cut out, or greatly shortened, as the movie would constantly slow down anytime the plot had to cut back to them. More time, instead, should've been devoted to Rey training with Luke Skywalker, and the mystery surrounding her backstory. There's also a little too much focus on certain animals and other alien creatures that don't really contribute much of anything, and are seemingly there just to sell toys. The strongest aspect, really, is the characters themselves. Leia gets to do a lot more and actually use her Force abilities, and Poe gets an arc wherein he learns that his hot headedness isn't always the best course of action. However, Finn is a bit underdeveloped in comparison to everyone else, other than striking up a possible new romance with Rose, and confronting Captain Phasma, who is once again underutilized and is....just sort of there. The greatest character moments lie in Luke Skywaker, who has become disheartened with himself and what's happened to the Jedi, with Rey willing to do anything to help him regain his hope. We also learn a ton more about Kylo Ren and his reasoning for turning to the Dark Side, and the odd sort of bond he and Rey strike up is not only interesting, but leads to the film's overall message of how sometimes failure can be the greatest teacher of all. So while the concepts this film introduces and the lessons it teaches are thought provoking, some of the side trips it takes the audience on leaves a bit to be desired, and overall, I feel both "Force Awakens" and "Rogue One" were much better paced. None the less, it still left me excited to see this story's conclusion, and what might eventually become of our favorite galaxy that's far, far away.

history.text: This movie is a combination of 2001 and Contact. Things do not happen in sequential order like we're used to seeing. This is not a linear movie. Do not assume that the first part of the movie is the present. If you really pay close attention during the last part of the movie you'll find it all comes together. The key to the story comes to fruition in her final conversation with Colonel Chang. If you miss it, watch the movie again.

Other than that small inconvenience it's well worth the money. Nobody, I mean nobody plays Miss Marple as well as Jane Hickson. history.text: I've got nothing but good opinions about sections 1, 3 and 4. They all are narrated by Rudy Maxa superbly. However, section 2 leaves much to be desired. The video is okay except it's on 5x4 format. The narration however is really amateurish. The music often drowns out the narrator and frequently the narrator is drowned out by people talking on the video itself. Had Rudy Maxa done section 2 the entire thing would have been superlative.
