history.title: Kingsman 2: The Golden Circle
history.text: "Kingsman: The Golden Circle" is a spy-spoof based on the 2012 comic book "The Secret Service" by Mark Millar and Dave Gibbons. An all-star cast completes this sequel to the 2015 original hit movie.Returning for episode 2 is Taron Egerton(very good), Colin Firth, and director Matthew Vaughn. "Kingsman: The Golden Circle" features great location shot, Bondlike gadgets, wild action, and crude humor. Gentleman Eggsy(Taron Egerton) appears outside of his tailor shop spy-HQ in London, when he is suddenly attacked by an old Kingsman training reject, and his new cyborg arm. A terrific deadly fight continues in a taxi racing through the night streets of London.Later that night, a bomb destroys the Kingsman's tailor shop headquarters and almost all the agents are killed. The bombing is traced to an international drug cartel called the Golden Circle, run by the smarmy nut-job known as Poppy(Julianne Moore), who lives in a remote jungle surrounded by 1950's retro decor; guarded by a small army of soldiers and robots. A scandal for the American president blurs the story in the second half, as political demagoguery takes over. "Kingsman" also stars Mark Strong, Halle Berry, Elton John, and Jeff Bridges as Champ. Julainne Moore easily steals the entire movie as Poppy, the devilish, funny head of the the Golden Circle drug cartel. A few key scenes include Elton John in pink feathers playing his trademark grand piano, and a flashy sequence of an out-of-control cable car crashing down the snow-covered Italian Alps. Matthew Vaughn, who has already helmed 6 movies, has been announced as director of "Kingsman 3". At 141 minutes, "Kingsman: The Golden Circle" is too long. But it's funny, and as chic and sharp as Taron Egerton's new suits.

history.title: Janis Joplin - Janis Little Girl Blue
history.text: Five stars. Up. Way up. Janis Joplin was a country girl from Port Arthur, a little hick-town in Texas. She was fat. She had acne. Her face was round. It was the 1950's, and boys made fun of her. They laughed at her. They made her cry. Life sucked. Then she and some friends got to Austin. Wow! Music in the air. Fun. You didn't have to be a babe. And little Janis found out she could sing. Even bluegrass. Janis and some friends got to Los Angeles. A new world. Music. Nice people. You didn't have to be a babe. It was 1964. Back and forth, Janis traveled from Texas to California, back and back again. She went to San Francisco. She started singing in little bars. She smoked pot. She had a few drinks. The big break for Janis Joplin was the Summer of Love, 1967, 50 years ago. It was the Monterey Pop Festival. Boom. Janis became a star at age 25. A whole new world. Janis found out she was happy on a stage singing the blues. And all those kids sitting out there listening. They were happy too...."Janis. Little Girl Blue" is a sad, beautiful rock-and-roll love story. So well done. So real. Interviews and scenes with Jerry Garcia, John Lennon, Bill Graham, and TV talk-show host Dick Cavett. And more. Her friends. Her lovers. Her managers. She could not know that the road would be short. Blasting out at Woodstock and the Avalon BallRoom, little Janis could not know that she would join the "27 Club", a list of famous artists would died at age 27(Hendricks, Morrison, and Janis). "Janis. Little Girl Blue" is a rare documentary, a true story of a sad little fat girl, who did good. And then saw it all fade away. A tear will come into your eye. You'll realize that life is short. But it's a gift. A gift to be alive.

history.text: If you enjoy watching movies, asking 'WTF just happened???' about 20x with never any clarification, then this movie's for you! I tried to enjoy it, but I couldn't help but wonder if being on some sort of heavy-duty drug might make the experience better. After the credits rolled, I went to the director's commentary for some intel. One of the first things said was along the lines of 'If Drive was like cocaine, then this movie's like heavy-duty acid.' Something like that. I don't do drugs, so . . . I'm out. There were some bright spots, however, and it was oddly satisfying to see an extremely ugly (on the inside) person deal with some pain. Not sure I want that to be the high-point of my movie-viewing experience, but there was definitely some sort of odd-honor-system going on with some of the characters, so who knows? Maybe I'll watch it again. After all, I do own it now. I will say that I watched it on a screen with defective lighting, so I may have missed some key elements . . . but I definitely prefer movies with more honor and fewer ethics-violations. Ymmv.

history.title: Those Daring Young Men In Their Jaunty Jalopies

history.text: The plot is basically a winner take all automobile race to Monte Carlo, with a love interest for Tony Curtis (Susan Hampshire) thrown in, which is set in the days between the two World Wars. The movie is along the same general lines as Those Magnificent Men in Their Flying Machines and if you enjoyed that movie you will probably like this one. Terry-Thomas is the foil for Curtis in this movie, and the acting is well done--especially Peter Cook as the British Army officer. You also get to see Gert Frobe (better remembered as Auric Goldfinger in the James Bond movie) in a comedy roll--which he carries off very well. Somewhat reminiscent of the Blake Edwards movie The Great Race (which I preferred to this one). Still--this movie is worth watching more than once. Both of these movies demonstrate that it is possible (if you want to) to make a funny movie without having to resort to profanity to get laughs.

history.title: WWE: WrestleMania XX
history.review_title: If I lost my copy of this---I wouldn't replace it---
history.text: I began watching the WWF about the time of WrestleMania II; primarily for the personalities and the interviews. To me, the matches themselves were always secondary. Promoters in the entertainment business are continually trying to ride the crest of the popularity wave, and this involves routinely making changes in format in attempts to capture new fans. Sometimes the changes produce the desired results; and sometimes they don't (see Brian France and NASCAR) and result in the loss of a portion of their already established fan base. I began to lose interest in the WWF about the time of the Stone Cold Steve Austin era, when there was a shift in the type of "personality" that management was looking for in their entertainers. For a while, I switched to WCW, but as that evolved, I eventually stopped watching altogether. I bought this DVD because of some of the individual personalities on the program, and once I had watched their matches, my interest in the program ended. Advice: Check out the lineup of matches; if there are wrestlers there who you enjoy watching--consider buying the DVD. If you are more interested in the personalities of the Saturday Night Main Event era-- buy one of the WrestleManias from that time period.

history.title: Vacation (HD/UV/BD)
history.text: I borrowed this movie from my local library based on the title and the concept. My intention was to see if I would enjoy it enough to purchase the DVD. The basic concept was alright, and there were actually one or two laughs during the hour and a half, but overall it was a major disappointment. This film compares to the original VACATION movie about like the SON OF THE PINK PANTHER compares to the PINK PANTHER films that starred Peter Sellers. The film reinforces various stereotypes, and the younger brother is such a brat that the movie would have been better if his character had been written out from the very beginning. A lot of vulgarity which didn't seem to serve any purpose, and while it was nice to see Chevy Chase and Beverly D'Angelo again, I don't believe either one of them will consider this one of their finer roles. It gets two stars based on the one or two funny moments---otherwise it is a one star effort at fulfilling a potentially promising concept.

history.title: Come Back, Little Sheba
history.review_title: Mother and Son and no way to suspend DISBELIEF...........
history.text: Well, not quite-------for awhile you offer it hope and continue hoping that you will get past this EGREGIOUS mistake, but.....alas, you finally give up, and it is the greatest reason for which the movie falls apart. Burt Lancaster was a handsome, almost beautiful man at the time this CURIOUS, engaging and ultimately disappointing film was released in 1952. He was 39, and perhaps the word "stud" was not insulting in the least. He exudes sheer masculinity, and a body that was muscular and virile. Shirley Booth was 54 at the time, and although there was much talk about the difference in age, they still went ahead and filmed it. Indeed, she won the Oscar for her performance and perhaps, only relying on her acting here, and not her competition that year, which I am not aware of, she perhaps most certainly deserved it. Her acting is compelling. The problem of 15 years of difference in age between a romantic, or married couple is not a problem at all, if: It is known to us that it is indeed clearly stated in the story. OR, as it has happened countless times the couple are totally convincing as close enough in age, no matter the difference so that there is little to doubt or "disbelieve" in the unfolding of the story. The third logical excuse for it is, of course, prostitution in any of the myriad ways in which it has been presented again and again in the movies, when the difference in age is vast. And then , of course, although rarely seen in film, but leaving aside cynicism, the reality in life that indeed two people of great difference in age do find love, in whatever manifestation to carry on a beautiful relationship. But that is not the case in this film. Both characters are, we are told, a pair that eloped perhaps decades ago for which we are to believe that they were two young adults, the female indeed never forgiven by her father to the present day, when they are perhaps, arguably in their forties or early fifties. Congratulations to all those who are able to get past such a profound flaw in casting, and DO suspend disbelief and carry on. That is not possible to one who is watching, studying the scenes closely enough, and trying for awhile to BELIEVE. The reason for that hope is that both Lancaster and Booth give excellent performances that make it all the more disappointing to deal with this impasse. Other flaws permeate in this movie, engrossing during perhaps the first hour (out of 2) and complex in the characterization of an alcoholic who has been sober for a year, and who clearly no longer?----loves his wife. She herself is living in the past, as he cruelly tells her repeatedly when she remembers their early love, passion, and ultimately the reason for which Lancaster "had" to marry her, having made her pregnant and obliged to fulfill his "duty" (perhaps we should be better off a society if we go back to that?) No chance. It appears to be assumed that he has apparently never loved her, in any romantic way, and has suffered for it all these years. SHE has clearly lived in blindness when it comes to their relationship, whatever remains of it. He treats her more like a mother----and again we are even more reminded of the flaw already discussed. At one point, you STOP caring. A young, supposedly wholesome college girl in need of a room is taken by Booths' character and this is the "excuse" for which everything seems to unravel. She is suddenly seen to be a rather "loose" girl, and Lancaster's character finds himself unexpectedly confronting his LUST for her. Naturally, an alcoholic who has just celebrated his first year of sobriety at A.A. is almost certainly to be a deeply fragile human being, and fighting his emotions he reaches for "the bottle"--------LITERALLY........ We all know that the last thing you need to have at hand when you are fighting those hideous urges that paralyze you when maintaining your sobriety is, well, should we bother to mention? Yes, indeed, having your poison within reach. And then you fall into MELODRAMA, because the IDIOTIC idea of having a bottle of liquor in the cupboard a few paces away from you is not something that any serious person in recovery will do------not to mention your loving wife, who goes crazy when suddenly the bottle has disappeared and she realizes that he has broken his pathetic sobriety. REALLY???..... Well, no, we are not idiots here, and we presume that THEY, rather intelligent people, notwithstanding their terrible inner lives, would not be either. That puts an end to the respect we have for the film. The end itself is totally anti-climactic. They are both children holding onto each other, and we should assume that they will try again. These last scenes, even at the end reinforce the idea of a mother-son relationship. Again, there is nothing absurd about that, in and of itself, but to go back to the beginning of my review, what we cannot forgive is the fact that "outside" of the "reality" of the movie, we have the reality of the movie's construction, so to speak. And nobody is able to convince me that this matronly woman 15 years her husband's senior is for us to be fooled by unless indeed the story offers us the fact that there was INDEED a difference in age. Wonderful performances, mediocre plot, and DETAILS of that plot that are unimaginable to accept within the "internal" logic of the movie. And Little Sheba? The lady's dog who disappeared, never to be found again, and nothing more than another excuse for the character's profound melancholy.

history.title: Funny Girl
history.text: This complicated drama took a loooong time to finally reveal its minor moments of near-greatness. Again, clearly a vehicle for Streisand, the movie curiously ends with what you probably would want to call an early version of a music video, as Barbra sings directly to the camera, a background all black, and at her most glamorous, where audience disappears and our protagonist is suddenly the star. I mean the protagonist as in Ms. Streisand, nothing to evoke images of the real Fanny Brice. But who was Fanny Brice? My partner, 11 years my senior, was able to fill in a few details, and I resisted going to Google before writing this review, but he tells me that much of it is a gloss of what the real Fanny Brice is all about. Nothing new or unusual in that other-worldly place called Hollywood, with its own histories and liberties. Does it matter? To a point, depending on how attached you are to the life and career of Brice will you be happy or disturbed. I am afraid that very few of us, except those in their late 60's, 70's, etc. will recall much about Ms. Brice. As well, those highly cultivated in the world of entertainment in the early part of the 20th. century will remember. So I guess it was easy to take license. I have to confess that I have never liked Streisand. She never got rid of that dreadful "Brooklyn-ees" (?) accent of the lower classes of the city and never came to reach a level of cultivation, of worldliness that I would have expected. To me she remained as plain as "steak and potatoes",so to speak----(and the steak, very, very well-done). She was unmistakably a very good singer, yet nothing truly unique like Holiday or Simone, and as far as I have read and bits that I seen, the projects in which her acting was tested later on , from the seventies on, turned out to be "middle-of-the-road", crude productions that have nothing to do with art. Yet she ultimately gives an all-around solid performance in this film. It is one of a deeply neurotic, fragile woman, dependent too much on the love of a man who clearly abuses her, uses her, and ultimately makes you believe that he has not truly loved her. But much of the movie is a sanitized bit of entertainment that fails to come across with profundity at all. It isn't unfair to comment on personal details like looks when you are a star as big as Streisand. The fact is that, although admirable that she decided not to reduce the size of her nose, that nose is almost a liability in itself, since you cannot stop looking at it, and not because it's beautiful. As well, she was (is?) cross-eyed, which makes some closeups a bit painful to look at. I have no idea, yet, who where the contenders for Best Actress that year, but my assumption is that they were rather "lightweights" when it came to serious, enlightening work. By itself, she alone, again, does convey a certain multifaceted quality that ultimately convinces you of the few, very fine moments in her work. Omar Sharif "almost" steals the picture from her, but she must have gone insane in fighting for this not to happen, which it does not, yet Sharif, with his exotic eyes and "mystery" provide a captivating series of moments that attempt to surpass her. Again, whatever number of gifted individuals put their efforts into this (and there are many names that escape me right now, but a lot of greatness in their arts) whether consciously or not, clearly conceived the picture thinking of whatever ways to make Streisand shine, not anything to do with a true interest in offering the public any light on the life and career of Fanny Brice. Quite a disappointment, and although my bias about Streisand the person could be used as an accusation against these notes, I am satisfied with the level of objectivity I place into this critique of a clearly failed production. Ah------one more caveat: 2 HOURS of moments of quality entertainment among a, dare I say, an extra half-hour of inanities and waste.............

history.title: The Deer Hunter DVD
history.review_title: A film only tangentially related to the Vietnam war
history.text: Indeed....... a three-hour movie that should have been cut to perhaps two, indulgent with an entire hour of blue collar life and all the pathetic sights of men who never, truly NEVER, outgrew their childhoods, and the machismo that accompanied that, what with their treatment of their women, there are long periods in which you want to say--------"All right, jump to Vietnam!!" (this because your writer had seen the movie originally in 1981, and at that time, at the age of 19 was totally taken by it.......indeed, the scenes of russian roulette and deNiro's grotesque laughter while fighting for his life I recalled countless times again and again)...... But that was THEN........ I should have bought some ILLUSIONS for tonight's 2nd. viewing--------which has proven to unfortunately unveil itself to be what is clearly a mediocre movie...... It never coalesces entirely----it is too fragmented. Unquestionably, the Vietnam torture scenes---------which again, have nothing in itself to do with Vietnam specifically--------are the heart of the movie. Have you ever seen a film that captivated you with its THEME SONG?.........In this case, not really a song, but what we may call a "motif" which returns to haunt you again and again in multiple variations by BACH (KIDDING!)-------by John William and leaves you with a feeling that stays with you for much longer than the movie? It's happened to me countless times, but in this particular case it appears almost SUPERIOR to the movie---at times, being so evocative in all its sadness. If plot is a mess, then we can be happy to say that acting is quite superb. All the performances are extraordinary, and two things were a surprise and one a "revelation". An actress who, unfortunately had been caught in that bizarre thing called "Mommie Dearest" plays a wonderful character here, RUTYANA _________ (I am embarrassed that only two hours have gone by and her last name escapes me......) The other is Meryl Streep, in all the naturalness of her youthful acting before she became the queen of the MIMICS, of MIMESIS.........Not of Interpretation, no, but of copying a personality's voice, movements, gestures and offering them to us as some sort of extraordinary performance. The Meryl Streep we see here, and a bit later in that harrowing film "Sophie's Choice" has left us long ago. The ravages of war in a personality before Psychiatry had invented the term "Post-traumatic-stress-disorder" (remember "Shell-shocked"?) are rendered, well, let's just say that although they are there, they do not satisfy. A director's mistake, perhaps? Do see the movie. Nothing to do with Vietnam, and only thrilling enough for all you "sado-Masochists" out there (in here too) in the viciousness of that monstrosity that society's structure keeps in check for most of us. A warning: those with upper-class pretensions should skip the first ENTIRE hour or they will start having too much guilt, or too much boredom and sneering at the antics of a bunch of people who even in a wedding can behave like animals.............

history.title: The People vs. Larry Flynt
history.text: Given all those negative words, the positives are impossible to forget-------and the fact is that that REPULSIVE woman by the name of Courtney Love gives a fantastic performance that perhaps------only perhaps-------manages to eclipse the GREAT performance by Harrelson. Or was Ms. Love simply playing herself?, as my companion wisely noted! Has she done any more acting? I do not know whether this was filmed before the death of her husband, but tell me if I am wrong-----I believe she became a very wealthy woman after that since she inherited most of Cobain's estate, so arguably because of that she never pushed herself----- and nothing to deter talent (very broadly speaking) than being very wealthy. Where do you think some acquaintances of mine ended? Not as leaders and great successes, but "losers" that quietly pursued "careers" that were purely imagination------aaah! those days when in certain circles nobody asked you "What do you do?". But perhaps we are better off today. The director carries us on a rollercoaster ride that can't stop or slow down since perhaps there wasn't a good screenwriter to give the movie depth. The film remains basically a "telenovela" (our new preferred way for "soap opera" that-----no offense to fans of "Days of our lives"--------begin and end within six months or so.......and the HEAT they emanate!!) But I digress----forgive me. Everything is just about "by the book", so to speak, but there's a lifeless quality to the structure of the whole act. Again, performances are STRONG, and they help us along the way, but then all this "OPERATIC", ridiculous music in so many scenes give a cheap grandiosity to the whole thing. Ludicrous----- just as ludicrous as the idealized portrait of Mr. Flynt himself. Basically a repugnant human being, Harrelson is here to give us a glamorized, falsified version of Flynt. Can you tell me how is it that in Bio-pics the protagonist is always so good-looking next to the real thing? Can't they find UGLY people just as in this case? Well, the fact is that there is a moment when FLYNT himself plays a very conservative, bloated judge that must have been a fantastic time for him (and US as well!). Of course, you need to recognize Flint, and this is roughly 20 years ago. Not to forget! Edward (?) NORTON, looking fresh as a kid out of High School, already had the wonderful skills that he was to prove to us over the years again and again. The movie's CORE and ------mistake?-------is the issue of the First Amendment. The reason why Flynt wins the case, at the Supreme Court no less, is because of a fake advertisement on his HUSTLER magazine in which that master of reincarnation of Jesus Jerry Falwell appears having sex with his mother. It is something ugly that you or I would not want to be humiliated by in our own lives. But the First Amendment, that mostly dormant one (?) in our magnificent constitution until, perhaps, "Larry Flynt VERSUS....." (or is my history correct?) brings Flynt to triumph when invoked convincingly enough so that what is basically a parody can be protected from Libel, etc. That has come to have serious positive (and not so positive) changes in our society's freedom of speech. The perplexing thing is that to a great extent that has nothing much (please tell me otherwise) to do with Flynt's dramatic fights with Justice over PORNOGRAPHY. Of course, the first amendment has, perhaps since then, opened the door to free distribution of Porn all across America (not to mention the NET and its intractable "problem" over whether we can limit or not the gigantic amount of PORN that has become the norm, and for which, quite seriously speaking, has made Flynt's publications almost a work of literature, no?). The movie simply shifts course and from Pornography itself it jumps to the protection of parody and anything you want to say about any public figure no matter how disgusting AS LONG as you inject some kind of tongue-in-cheek. Am I right that a program like "Saturday Night Live" was greatly improved by this decision? Perhaps you can guess that one subject follows the other, but it is an obscure connection that perhaps someone reading this can illustrate for us. For that, Mr. Flynt will be remembered------surprisingly enough that the decision was unanimous, in a court eternally divided 5-to-4. That is perhaps too much "thinking" to try to inject into this, again, failure of a course on LAW, but even without it the film remains a mash-up of biography--------not to mention that this "moderate" (your writer) found it extremely celebratory of its liberal viewpoint, unfairly leaving us in the dark (irresponsibly so) about the counter-arguments. Mr. Norton exudes wisdom in his defense, but NO ONE does for Conservatism. Terrible history, moderately exciting entertainment.

history.title: Repulsion (The Criterion Collection) [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: Deneuve in a MAGNIFICENTLY MAGNETIC Performance......
history.text: Deneuve literally CHEWS up the movie. And that brings us to consider the role of a director when it comes to a movie like this. Clearly, being her second role since being catapulted to stardom with that ridiculous "musical" The Umbrellas of..........( the French NEVER understood the meaning of a Musical), she must have been "directed" for this by Polansky, the EPHEBOPHILE. But how much credit should a director take when having cast such a superior actor as MS. Deneuve? If there is any honesty in him------very LITTLE. A marvelous example is BRANDO-----perhaps the epitome of "self-directing"-----you did not direct Brando, and you knew it from the beginning. She, clearly, so early in her career was not Brando, and some actors, no matter their brilliance rely on their director to act in whatever way they "should". But, again, with work such as this one I don't believe that such a performance was "created" by Polansky. Do you find that this opinion is mistaken? The movie has dated a bit. Scenes like the one where arms come out of the walls made us (the group that were watching it at home last night) titter and snort. This only happened once, Thanks be to the Gods. But it is borderline-farcical. What is curious to me (will you call me a Macho misogynist?) is that up until we see the deterioration of her character into what is clearly a sad, pathetic psychotic, deluded victim I have a great compassion for her, but after the first killing my heart grows cold and I no longer have the slightest pity for this poor woman. The fact that it is the (beautiful) man in love with her contributes to this, and the fact that she kills the landlord in such a vicious way renders her repugnant to my VISCERAL MIND-------let us stress visceral, since my intellect recognizes the hopelessness of what drives her to this. Her profound depression leading to this is heartbreakingly sad. For a while we played with motive, until we "patched it together", so to speak, and kind of convinced ourselves that those scenes in which she clearly is being raped are the key that Polansky offers us as perhaps rather simplistic an answer as to WHY. What is not so easy to interpret is the monster behind it all. Polansky gives you a SLY moment that, indeed, had us recoil and be surprised and, yes, REPULSED at that grotesque smile that only appears on the sister's lover for a moment. And so you have to, perhaps, come to the conclusion that HE is the perpetrator of these repugnant acts. BUT IS HE? We will never know---I doubt that Polanski has "confessed" it during an interview, He need not have been---------he may have lusted after her for long, she ignoring him, and he, a piece of filth, enjoys her tragedy. By the way, the woman who plays the sister offers us an unforgettable performance to rival Deneuve, particularly when she falls apart upon the discovery of the corpse. Why 3 stars instead of 4? A kind of stingy "It's Okay"?..... I hesitated with 4, but there is an element of "terror" film, of "HORROR" genre that robs the film of the potency of Ms. Deneuve 's performance. Perhaps the movie needed RESTRAINT, from which he could not, well, RESTRAIN himself so that thinking of MONEY he "sells out" to a mass audience. A great work of "entertainment" that fails to uncover the PROFOUND issues that can destroy a personality, a human being's core to, as in this case (by no means, as we know, the response of the majority of women that are raped) to its disintegration. The film tries, but perhaps it is to a certain degree an impossibility. I have been pondering what my very greatest GENIUS of film, Bergman would have done with the subject. Still, to be 19 (as she was at the time) and give as difficult and complex a performance as this is to be remembered for always. She must remain proud over this achievement. NOT SO with Mr. POlanski.

history.title: Callas Forever [DVD]
history.review_title: Mr. Zeffirelli's failure of a Paean to CALLAS..............
history.text: It is fascinating to find that 94% of the reviewers of this film here at Amazon rate it 2 to 4 stars (from "it's OK" to "I love it") to a movie that is a dull travesty, a ludicrous film, 120 minutes of which only the last 30 approach anything remotely to be considered inspiring. And remember that Ms. Callas was Zeffirelli's best friend, or one that bewitched him. The grotesque joke is that the premise of the film is based on what can be magnificent fuel to all of Callas' enemies----and they are infinite. The basic "contraption" is that Callas is despondent, a recluse, it is 1977 (the same year that she dies) and her close friend, a film director, convinces her to go into the studio and lip-synch arias from "Carmen" as an actual cinematic story (not a concert). She goes along with the concept, very reluctantly for a long while. The "joke" as I say, is that Callas was, and continues to be considered an ACTRESS, not a great singer by any possibility, by many, many people who do not understand and cannot recognize the profundity of her art. I myself, a great Callas fan since I heard her voice in film (cannot remember) where she was singing "Addio del Passato" from Traviata, recognized a voice that was not, decidedly the beautiful voice of Victoria de los Angeles, by any chance, and yet moved me to tears with her delivery. A friend and I have had countless arguments about this. And people continue to. The FACT is that, yes, the voice was imperfect, and she was an actress (and what an actress, from what I read, and snippets that I have seen that do not exactly convey this reasoning) but more than an actress thanks to her physicality, her acting was the VOICE itself. The greatest of opera singers are not the ones who deliver the highest notes but those that can simply utter a phrase with so much humanity, so much wisdom that they are incomparable. That was Callas. With this lip-synching that she is convinced to do Zeffirelli, again, is telling us that, after all, we can unite the recordings with her great acting, which she purportedly still has and presto! we have a magnificent movie. But Callas was an artist of the greatest dignity and standards and this whole thing would turn out to be a ridiculous pantomime. It is even "sadder" since you have three actors of very high caliber: Joan Plowright, Fanny Ardant, and Jeremy Irons. All of them go through the paces with the most ridiculous of screenplays. Ms. Plowright has to deliver lines like: "This is 1977----Satan is redundant". The mediocrity is everywhere. Perhaps it isn't surprising, as I just discovered that, along with some great moments as a director, hideous things like "The Blue Lagoon" with Brooke Shields are part of his "repertoire"---not to mention a rather recent fiasco with his staging of "Tosca" at the Met in NY. No, I think that Callas would have been deeply dissatisfied with this "paean" to her: he certainly could have thought something better. Not to mention that Fanny Ardant does not look AT ALL like a woman who is about to die of a heart attack within months! She looks magnificent, the very portrait of health, and by then Callas was a broken woman. Of course, it is all fantasy, but you are stretching the truth with this. As well, this man does the very unimaginative thing to act as if this is the 1950's, when every movie had to have a love affair inserted no matter the subject, and so does he, showing his lack of imagination: Irons is gay, but being 2002 Zeffirelli decides NOT to have Irons' young male stud even share a kiss, and Callas herself has a tentative moment with her lead from the picture---this is all thrown in as nothing more than filler. Again, it is simply unimaginable that any great artist, as dignified and with an ego the size of a supernova (which she has been since, say 1950) would have in any way accepted the ludicrous project of acting out a movie moving her lips to the recordings that made her the international star she remains, without breaking down. Let me put it to you this way: the GREATEST moment in the film is the credits as they slowly roll by........why is that??? Callas sings "Vissi D'Arte" from Tosca in the background and it is a moment where you know that every Callas fan remained seated unlike all the other movies where everyone, rather rudely, runs for the door. That hands it to you in a nutshell.............

history.title: Hello, Dolly!
history.review_title: Aaah, the MUSICAL, that "forgotten" art now called "Spiderman"...............
history.text: I did not grow up with the Musical.....I am 52, but my partner is 64 and he has beautiful memories of going to Broadway in the mid-60's and early 70's UNTIL Mr. Stephen Sondheim appears on the scene, RE-CREATES, contradicts, re-invents, and some say DESTROYS the musical. My partner does not have fond feelings for him. For Rodgers and Hart, oh my! For Cole Porter, wow!-------and then there's Jerry Herman, perhaps the last gasp of the old wonderful, tender, silly musical that runs from, say, the 1920's to the 60's...... That "last gasp" would more or less be this......... You have very probably heard a teenager see any of these DINOSAURS and cluelessly say: "How ridiculous! People breaking into song in the middle of a conversation?!". Perhaps we should blame so-called "modernism" for its death-------among many other things that modernism has left us with---- like.......architecture?.......Well, I am NOT in any way against modernism---certainly not of "REALISM"-----neo-realism, or else---------those that taught us that "suspension-of-disbelief" was to be given in very minimal dosages..... Ad so we come to Ms. Streisand with those last gasps, indeed: "Funny Girl", a beautiful achievement, "Funny Lady" (not yet seen by me, but generally considered a mediocre product) and this...... I have never liked Streisand, never cared for that "Brooklynese" chatter that she displays here in all its glory, which we must assume that she simply decided never to "clean up" and be what she was. BRAVO for her! Bravo for that nose! (By the way, do you know the amount of talent that Brooklyn produced in the 20th century? It is staggering----all magnificently talented jews). But I think that rare is the person who will not warm up to this woman's tender voice. It is a voice where, interestingly, all that "vulgar" chatter and accent disappears, and she delivers her songs in a wonderful diction to begin with, extending all her SSSSS's to the infinite, and every word carefully enunciated. Her voice is beautiful, unique, humane, needful, sober, honest, heartbreaking...you can go on and on.....The arrangements are too sentimental a lot of the time, but even then she pierces you with that magnetism, that slow manner that sings truth. Here, the subject which I tried to present to you is in full display. It is exquisitely SILLY, a "turn-of-the-century" story in NYCity that is simply an excuse for Streisand to show us what a wonderful poseur she was in the sixties at a time when Rock and Roll was changing the culture, the very essence of music, coarse and revealing, vulgar and profound, and I don't know who went to these movies but I can safely assume that the audiences were mostly post-30's in their age?, certainly not teenagers and certainly not people listening to the Stones or Hendrix, or the Beatles' late work. The illusions were dead, the "suspension-of-disbelief" was no longer possible, broadly speaking, and again, the ridiculousness of dancing in the middle of a conversation, of a thin plot that demands very little attention defy your temper-----I left the room a number of times, coming back to the words of "don't worry, you did not miss anything"....Ha! And yet, it is moving in its own "passe" way----for us getting older it is almost more of a testament to the fact that everything will change and not even our own genres will subsist and time is pushing us away.....Don't talk to me about J-lo and Beyonce and even PATHETIC Madonna (who I grew up with!) at the age of 56 unable to transition into middle-age and showing us a sad human being trapped in a hollow image that insists on being sexual and "depraved" and all anew, ready to devour.... But...the movie. Again, depending on who you are, you may or may not have a good time. It is NOT the musical as an example of greatness, certainly not an example of the embodiment of the musical genre. There's a tiredness to it, an absurdity that wants you to say----"all right, enough!". It is, I believe, 2+ hours and yet as I write that I realize that it rarely lags. Walter Matthau is not my idea of a great leading man, unlike Rex Harrison accompanying Audrey Hepburn in "My Fair Lady", but it will have to do, no? There are almost no exceptional numbers, EXCEPT....yes, "Hello Dolly", but it is my confusion on whether "Hello Dolly" the song was a huge hit for Streisand, because for two decades I have heard it sung (not to mention "trumpeted"?) by Louis Armstrong in a marvellous way, an unforgettable way, yet here he is, thrown in awkwardly in the middle of a long musical scene and an audience who wouldn't have known him would be perplexed (not to mention that he is not playing) of the two of them together, he the ONLY BLACK person in the entire movie to be given anything of a role (historically correct, but also making you wonder whether this was done so that the segment could be excised in the south? In 1969?----I have no idea). Again, listen to Armstrong's version and the pure, sheer JOY of his delivery shake you to the core. I believe this was Armstrong's LAST hit (and a super-hit that topped the charts---in the middle of all that Rock and roll revolution) before his death. Watch the movie. But you will not be missing much, to be brutally honest, if you don't. A fan of Streisand? By all means. She delivers. For a "girl" in her late 20's to show so much poise, so great an amount of sophistication, class, acting skills, singing, of course----it makes you realize what a great talent we had here and how much we have descended to forty years later. Or is it old age slowly creeping up on me, and the pull of the past?................

history.title: Bonnie and Clyde (Two-Disc Special Edition)
history.text: For a long while you fear sitting down to watch this movie, since you have been (mis)led to believe it to be a work of consummate ART (caps required). You need not fear. Tonight I sat down to two hours of magnificent VACUITY that ends up with that closing shot which makes you laugh out loud, since it is considered to be the "breakthrough" moment in american cinema which led to the explosion of all that violence which came to be necessary to attract middle-brow audiences thirsty for blood, and you realize how out of proportion such a statement is. Well, good for all those "scholars" who find such a trajectory an action of great importance. But the movie ITSELF is a complete disappointment. The first thing that came out of my mouth while quietly at home with friends and not having to be pestered by "Sssshhh"s when at the theatre was "What an irresponsible movie!". But that soon led to the exquisitely TEDIOUS scene after scene of the same cheap stuff. Again and again, poor sad human beings are subjected, during the Depression to the indignities of being robbed of their pennies (and lives, as it progresses). Mr. Penn proves himself to be exquisitely unimaginative with his constant rat-tat-tat of bank after bank, with blood delightfully presented in "joyously" cosmetic form. True, what could he do but film the pathetic story of these two white-trash individuals, who just happen to be made beautiful by Hollywood (who wants to see UGLY people when dealing with a "fun ride" in which you need as much aesthetics (very minor ones---let us not confuse the word with that seriou and rich area of Philosophy)--------as possible? So B. & C. are offered to us in the panoramic pair of beauty by the names of Warren Beatty (who, unimaginatively uses the same slow-motion cheap ending of this movie when many years later directing and starring in "Bugsy"---true genius, eh?) AND that great unique beauty Ms. Faye Dunaway-------and watch her mannerisms closely to realize the short range of this actress as you are remember again and again that those same moves are in full bloom 12 years later with "Mommie Dearest" (unquestionably, and bizarrely so the best acting job of her precarious career). If we are to have trash occupy space it better be beautiful and stylish. That SOIGNEE "Park Avenue" hair on Bonnie, a hick that barely can speak a proper sentence! Those magnificent eyes and smile in that nobody named Clyde! It is true that both offer us a pleasurable ride throughout more than a bit of the film, acting that is mannered and self-conscious (read: impossible to suspend disbelief), and that to be honest everyone behaves beautifully in their acting jobs. It is also true that, new to me, the idea of a man suffering from impotence during his "best" years, especially one who is to be such a "lady-killer" as Clyde, suddenly brings to us a moment of deep reflection on what agonies such men must have gone through. And it is very tender to watch Bonnie embrace it all after an initial disappointment---not to mention his "triumph" in finally being able to "perform" for once towards the end----his ego seemingly so inflated that at last he can sustain an erection---power, as we know, can activate hormones that have perhaps been blocked by trauma for decades, even. In that way, the director (but really Clyde's story itself?---or just another intent in humanizing his characters?) offers us an opportunity to feel deeply (those who will) for such YOUNG men suffering from such a sad condition, and when considering that Cialis, Viagra and that incredible injection (mmmm....) were not around then. But we were not able to feel anything for Clyde---the physical condition displayed makes all of us highly successful men in such matters (allow me.....ha!) feel great compassion. But the plot cannot go anywhere---it is simply, and unbelievably TEDIOUS to watch robbery after robbery and have us lose our patience as we start counting. No matter the distractions and shallow changes from bank to bank, no matter the thousand chases and stolen cars---------whoever is enlightened by such a plot is to be commended..,....... The characterizations, as much as the acting is brilliant in its own way, are EMPTY, SHALLOW, deeply STUNTED throughout------throw the book of synonyms at it. You won't be wrong. The iconization of violence while insisting that these are "good" human beings takes us nowhere. We learn NOTHING whatsoever about Bonnie and Clyde--------perhaps their true story is the real thing, so to speak. What Mr. Penn tries to convey, it clearly comes across is that every "monster" inside of us is also a human being. Well, we know that from having read history and realized that even grotesque "heroes" like Napoleon and Alexander were ALSO human. I won't go as far as Mr. H..... (in the 20th century) because I have too much respect for my Jewish friends, but the truth is that what Penn tries to convey and HUMANIZE but fails UTTERLY is really, ultimately, alas......an empty PAGEANT of people going nowhere AND developing not one single bit. This is a magnificent example of what has repeatedly happened again and again throughout history: a few people cluelessly offering pathetic opinions metastasizes into a gigantic metaphor for something that carries no substance whatsoever at its core. It is, to an extent, if a bit much here for the term, a sort of minor propaganda. And it works so much of the time as it has here. Mild entertainment, especially for its ridiculous "slow-motion" ending which brings laughter and titters to all in the room........

history.title: The Gospel According to St. Matthew
history.review_title: Neo-Realism at its crudest, most stilted, ineffective, indeed irresponsible manifestation.....
history.text: If all the actors in this ridiculous movie were indeed non-actors, this time it did not work. To counter critics of the severity of my review, you find elsewhere, if you care, my review of Mamma Roma.....I consider it a 5-star masterpiece. The greatness of neo-realism resides in its combination of great acting skills (the great Anna Magnani in a heartbreaking performance) and a myriad of non-actors that give a certain curious challenge to the portrayal of everyday.life. Having said that, we know that most of can sustain, given the right direction a scene or two in a role that is not too demanding. That is because we spend our entire lives ACTING, whether consciously OR unconsciously, and to different degrees of narcissism (not to mention success!). Even the homeless person on the street has "memorized" his "stump speech"----let us not go there what with the present endless debate in America and its "artful" politicians. In this case, out of sheer arrogance or some stupid idealism Mr. Pasolini decided to dedicate more than 2 hours to one of the most taxing, cheaply pseudo-intellectual of all films in memory----and I have watched the very finest in the long history of American and international Cinema. The movie was clearly made on pennies (not in itself a liability), and the direction is appalling. One sad thing that comes to mind, heartbreakingly so is that all of these peasants ( were they all?)---apart from the figure of Jesus must have unquestionably been paid a pittance for their work-----and of course, Pasolini went on to reap the rewards and not give one single thought about sharing any proceeds with these poor souls.. Aesthetics: Surely, 2,000 years ago there were no dentists, but the fact that Mr. Pasolini chooses the most grotesque of "smiles" is an act of manipulation and nothing else. The fact that PIER selects the UGLIEST of faces (or more to the point the lighting that makes them look monstrous) is yet another manipulative effect, all in the name of "realism"........This is no critique of beauty versus ugliness, this is about steering your audience towards shock value. I grew up "catholic" (big quotes) and every Good Friday we were given the same ration of Hollywood, Cecil B. Demille drivel (not without its cheesy pleasures). I cannot say these were not at least VISUALLY beautiful (say, "Song of Songs"), but that ends the whole of the aesthetics problem. On to the REAL merits of a film like this.... "Actors" begin by staring at the camera endlessly---------let us emphasize endlessly, but with the important caveat that NOTHING, virtually NOTHING offers us expressiveness. Indeed, what we contemplate are faces that are CLUELESS and baffled----baffled we start becoming as more and more of this develops. If you have no idea of the life of Christ, you will be given a greatly distorted view, Pasolini "artfully" rendered. The movie that I saw, om TV and pay-per-view was DUBBED, but I seriously DOUBT that the original italian was delivered in any different way (an analogy is Fellini's films, which are given a disemboweled feel to them, but mostly those from his "depraved" period where anything goes, the antithesis of this film). The lines are recorded in the studio, in a magnificently stilted way, virtually READ, and during all the passages where Jesus is to be at his most charismatic you know that NOBODY would have followed this FOOL. (We will not go into issues of historical revisionism since then there is no reason for this movie, as it has been proven quite effectively that Jesus is a figure of lore---indeed one of the greatest, most perplexing events in human history---and I am decidedly NOT a conspiracy theorist------but being an agnostic, none of that matters at all. The fact is that the Gospels are filled with an amount of humanism that unquestionably changed the world-------if taking centuries for such a thing to happen.. There is no doubt on my mind that Pasolini had seen all that Hollywood "trash" and decided to go to the opposite extreme. But when, not only do you have performers read their lines in a studio, BUT you leave large chunks of the story out, not to mention its greatest and most dangerous flaw, you know you are dealing with an inflated ego that wishes to supersede the historical cinematic past. The VIA CRUCIS (also known as the seven-stations of the cross---and I don't mean Mal Gibson's grotesque blood-fest!) is, perplexingly, left out entirely. This is one of the most beautifully humanistic moments in the history of Christ. More importantly, shiveringly so, is Pasolini's COMPLETE lack of nuance when dealing with the extraordinarily subtle issues that go into the outcome, which is that the Jews "kill" Jesus. To make it short, Jesus is a jew and the small jewish community is terrified of its master, ROME. Anything can tilt the events against the Jews. And suddenly this RABID, angry, violent, exquisitely megalomaniac man appears before them, creating mayhem. And...he refuses to show his main card, his miracles, to the Jewish establishment. I think that most of us, given such a context, and hanging by the skin our teeth, would have had him killed. The Jews are portrayed in the least sympathetic of ways. By the way, I am NOT Jewish, but have the greatest respect for them. ONCE AGAIN, in the history of so much media, an uncultivated person leaves the theater with the clear idea that the Jews killed Christ. Well YES, they actually convince the Roman authorities to kill one of them, a madman for all they know. A fellow JEW. Pasolini was a devoted Catholic------the magnificently bizarre contradictions of this film if he indeed was NOT an anti-semite prove THE FILM to BE anti-semitic-------not in any way blatantly so, but what do you get when growing with Mussolini?.......perhaps more than a few "snatches" of that monstrous' "intellectual" propaganda. As we have come to know more and more, a Marxist's agenda differs very little, ultimately, with that of a fascist's one...It took many of us to figure that one out, no? Castro, anybody? Pasolini was one more phony "Communist" reaping the benefits of very generous materialist comforts while spewing "equality" from a very safe place. It takes quite a compartmentalization to separate the artist from the BUFFOON. Finally, right after Christ's death there is no "recorded" earthquake that destroys the "favela" built on a hill. It is only a darkening of the skies which lead Roman soldiers to be perplexed and suddenly turn "Christian". Finally, those that will try to defend the film by way of insisting that this is the ".......according to St. Mark" and no more miss the point. When you align all four gospels---one next to each other------you can see that the differences are in NUANCE, not plot. That this work of UTTER MEDIOCRITY has been lauded over the course of 50 years or so, remains as problematic as Bunuel's "...discreet charm.........". This is an exercise in hubris, an amateur work, irresponsible, sadly anti-semitic, but most importantly when looking for inspiration from christianity and his leader will find you confronting, alas..........absolute STERILITY........... ASIDE: the movie contains, at different moments, the most beautiful seemingly African/Brazilian music. It is spellbinding, and I would be honored if anyone will send me a note telling me what it is if they know!

history.title: Malcolm X (Two-Disc Special Edition)
history.text: No question about it........ Yet, it is clearly an act of RACISM and, we must accept, perhaps Mr. Lee's "arrogant" ways that offer us the humiliating fact that the film was ignored for Best Picture OR Best Director............The brilliant, stunning performance of Denzel Washington/ Malcolm X (because he seemed to transform himself into X without the silly mimesis of that great actress who first gave us "Sophie's Choice" and then slowly descended into PARODIES) was the only nomination among the top--and he lost to "Mr. Scarface" for "Scent of a woman" or some sort of insignificant reel when compared. Angela Bassett is simply heartbreaking as his wife, and the very moment of the killing offers us a haunting display of agony, characterized by her cries of sorrow that are so chillingly extraordinary that they have haunted me to this day--------TWENTY-FIVE years later. The entire movie captures X in all the many shades of his persona and inner being. What may be considered controversial by some is Lee's exquisite handling of the main dilemma that remains: WHO killed Malcolm X---and he does it with great fairness, but leaves little doubt of the fact that although the FBI persecuted him, the ultimate responsibility is in the hands of that repugnant group "The Nation of Islam" and its magnificently corrupt leader ELIJAH MOHAMMED, with whom X bravely parts after finding the truth of HIS leader's own phoniness. The movie is a beautiful testament to Malcolm X's profound honesty and searing search for truth, culminating with the change that comes too late for the "world" to acknowledge---even to this day, when particularly white people (but I would bet that, alas so many BLACKS as well!) have no clue as to his transformation from his "hatred" of whites and his loud, damning speeches and reputation as a horrible counter-racist and even violence- inciting man of "God" (his ...."by any means necessary...") to a preacher, a humanist almost in tandem with the great Martin Luther. Not so arguably, every white American should see this film, to penetrate the very many layers of RACISM that to this day continue to haunt this nation-----------but, as well, what is a historically almost exact record of the life of this extraordinary person. Alas, not only should every White American, BUT every BLACK person, indeed among MANY who, as most people in America seem to regard History as unnecessary to their lives, living literally more and more detached from everything that has molded us. This is, I believe a 3+ hour film, yet it NEVER slows, never has us praying for it to end. BRAVO to Spike Lee for his gargantuan efforts, to Washington for his immersing into a complex character and capturing his many "selves"---------and ultimately, if outside of the film, of course to the great Malcolm X himself for his transforming being that leads to his own liberation and forgiveness, to whatever extent, of the generations of Americans who shared (and continue to!) the guilt of participation in what remains the greatest STAIN of this extraordinary nation.

history.title: Charles Gounod: Romeo et Juliette - Villazon/Machaidze
history.review_title: Don't waste you money. Don't waste your time, unless you like revisionist Euro-trash.
history.text: Wow, where do I start, with this one? I’m a big fan of Villazón and his singing is about the only thing I found redeeming about this performance. Nino Machaidze’s (Juliette) singing passes muster and I would give her a B+ but no more. Despite that, my patience and tolerance, for revisionist pap, was worn and I couldn’t finish watching the 2nd disc of this 2 disc presentation. I’m tempted to refer to this “performance” as Romeo and Juliette meet the three stooges, as directed by Dr. Frankenstein. There is so much about this performance which is just wrong. I guess we should start with the Act 1, which opens with a gang rape, all of the participants in which then calmly exit the stage while others segue, seamlessly, into a masked ball. Pure and gratuitous nonsense and irrelevance? Yes, to say the least. Then, we have the costuming, which remains, throughout the “performance.” The vast majority is French, 18th century foppish, intermixed with piratical dress and a few universal clown costumes. Juliette’s entry makes her look and act more like a ditzy, slightly slow-witted girl of 10 years of age. Villazón, as Romeo, wears a full length, black, leather coat, with tall, matching, black boots, which clothing looks like it might have been better assigned to a Nazi, secret police officer of the 1930s~40s. Throughout the performance, we are treated to “dinner-theater” quality activities of the performers, roaming about, in the audience and/or in the area between the orchestra pit and the audience. Also, throughout the performance, we are provided with a series of out-of-context fist fights and sword play. What don’t we have, in this performance? We don’t have a story line anywhere near what Shakespeare wrote or even contemplated might have been done. Buy, instead, the Roberto Alagna (Romeo) Leontina Vaduva (Juliette) performance.

history.title: Out of the Ashes
history.review_title: This movie should be seen, by anyone who is not sure that pure evil does exist.
history.text: This is a gritty, realistic and, from an historical perspective, reasonably accurate presentation, in the overall sense. Without question: 1) there was a female, Jewish, Romanian (not Hungarian, as portrayed, in this video) physician (MD), by the name of Gisella Perl, who was gynaecologist, as well as an inmate and survivor of Auschwitz; she was, also, an extensive abortionist, while there; 2) Josef Mengele was a physician (MD), anthropologist (PhD) and German Army SS officer, at Birkenau and Gross-Rosen (neither camp was mentioned, in this video), as well as in Auschwitz, where he earned the sobriquets of “butcher of Auschwitz” and “angel of death,” having performed, ordered and/or overseen uncountable numbers of “experiments,” on living inmates, without anesthetics; 3) the Holocaust did occur. There is overwhelming documentation of Mengele’s atrocities. The Nazi staff kept exacting and highly detailed records of all of Mengele’s and other concentration camp “experiments.” As to the specific details, regarding Dr. Perl’s actions and activities, as presented in this video, it would appear that many may have been “dramatized,” to fit the overall tone of the movie. Now, that’s not suggesting that what is presented, about her, did not occur, in the general sense. I’m merely suggesting that the sequence and many specifics are not confirmable, with any records, to support her, other than her memories, the memories of a few, other survivors and the documents Dr. Perl created, after she came to the US, seeking US citizenship and to practice medicine. Other details conflict with confirmed fact. For example, the point, at which she tries to poison herself, is depicted, in the video, as soon after arriving in Auschwitz and immediately after she realizes that Mengele is the animal she just unwittingly helped to gas a group of pregnant women. In reality, she did not attempt that suicide, until 1947, after she was released from Bergen-Belsen (she was transferred, there, after Auschwitz and before the Russian liberation of Auschwitz, another time-adjusted detail, in this video), when she became aware that her husband and son had died, in concentration camps. In this video, she is depicted as working in the wrong NYC hospital. She actually worked in Mount Sinai Hospital, after coming to the US, where she specialized in research on infertility treatments.

history.title: Lohengrin WWV 75
history.review_title: Not bad but not fully accurate or traditional
history.text: Anna Netrebko’s voice is still excellent and, while Piotr Beczala’s voice is very good, they do not produce the “magic,” of the combination of joint efforts of Netrebko and Rolando Villazón. Wagner’s situs, for this opera, is early 10th century Antwerp. The military and civilian costumes, for this performance, are more like that of WW2 France, especially the helmets of the soldiers. Some of the on-stage motion seems to take place, solely for the sake of motion and without purpose. Wagner’s ending calls for 1) a the swan to transform, again becoming Gottfried, the younger brother of Elsa, 2) a dove to descend, from heaven, then, taking the place of the swan, at the head of the boat, to lead Lohengrin to the castle of the Holy Grail, 3) Elsa, upon seeing her brother, whom she believed dead, to collapse, then die, while, 4) simultaneously, Ortud is pronounced guilty of witchcraft. In this version, 1) the swan remains, while Gottfried steps out of it, 2) I didn’t see any dove descend, 3) Lohengrin does not return to the castle of the Holy Grail and 4) Ortrud is not condemned for witchcraft. Overall, a well sung performance but not the best and it did not make the use of the available technology, to create the missing transformation scene. If you want a more traditional and better sung version, buy the Placido Domingo, Lloyd Robert, Cheryl Studer and Harmut Welkert performance, available from Arthaus Musik.

history.title: Verdi: Rigoletto [DVD]
history.text: This is a traditional production, albeit, with the audio and video quality typical of the early 1980s. Despite that, it’s well done, for the most part. I’m a big fan of Pavarotti but, in this part, at his then age, he did not provide a convincing, 20-something Duke of Mantua. The same can be said for Christiane Eda-Pierre, who, at the time of this performance, was 49~50 but looked substantially older and had a declining voice. She was way too old, to be playing the part of late-teens girl and Pavarotti too old, for the early twenties duke. Louis Quilico, on the other hand, not only made a perfect and convincing Rigoletteo but sang the role perfectly. The other players fit the bill acceptably. There aren’t a lot of quality productions of Rigoletto out there. The best I’ve seen, so far, is the Placido Domingo (Duke of Mantua), Cornel MacNeil (Rigoletto), Ileana Cotrubas (Gilda) production, from 1977. The worst, so far, is the Met’s 2014/15 production, which moved the venue to Las Vegas and the time period to the early 1960s. This production is one I would keep, since it is better than average and is a traditional performance.

What's most disturbing about this trend of home invasion films is the possibility (or likelihood?) of real-life copycat events and the de-sensitization of young minds to this brand of violence.

history.title: The Visit (DVD)
history.text: This latest offering from M. Night Shyamalan held my interest from the start to the finish and I rate it 4 stars because I think it is better than the 3-star average rating here. I wasn't sure what to expect considering it was from M. Night, who has received a lot of bashing over the past several films, and not always deservedly so, IMO. Anyway, I found this film both entertaining (the teen brother and sister were pretty good in their roles here) and creepy once the film gets about halfway in. What was the coolest part is the twist ending, which I didn't see coming. So, in summary, if you decide to pass on this because you assume it might be another Shyamalan bomb, you should keep an open mind and check it out anyway...you might be surprised. Definitely worth at least a rental.

history.title: Sekirei: Complete Series (Blu-ray/DVD Combo)
history.text: Sekirei is an Anime and Manga series that will entertain over and over again. I've owned this Anime for several years and can still watch it from beginning to end. This is one of those worlds you can escape into and experience the coming together of strangers who form close friendships and love for one another (Bonds) while trying to live a normal daily life and also contend with the challenges of The Sekirei Plan. The Sekirei Anime series was produced from July 2, 2008 to September 26, 2010. It includes 25 episodes and 2 OVA which were adapted from the Sekirei Manga [[ASIN:B017I271A4 Sekirei, Vol. 1]] chapters 1-73 (Volume 1-8) and chapters 98-107 (Volume 11). Anime fans are aware that Anime producers don't strictly adhere to the Manga's storyline so if you've seen the Sekirei Anime then you'll find surprises in the Sekirei Manga and visa versa. In addition to that, there are several sub-stories in the Manga that didn't make it into the Anime series. It seems the Sekirei Manga's publication (18 Volumes) couldn't keep up with the pace of the Sekirei Anime's production and so the Anime studio probably had to move on to produce other Anime series instead. Now that the Sekirei Manga is complete it would be nice to see another season or two of the remaining Sekirei saga produced to bring the Anime series to a conclusion.

There's only one lesbian character, but she does nothing but awkwardly grope a super-babe's crotch over her clothing. This video was an enormous disappointment for me. There's really no plot here. history.title: Sexy Warriors
history.review_title: People want to see beautiful amazon women with other women, but that's NOT what this one is about!
history.text: Director Dean McKendrick had a chance to make something really creative with this one, but I don't believe that his heart was in it. The two cover-girls on the DVD boxcover, Jazy Berlin and Erika Jordan, are both incredibly beautiful, as is pretty Christine Nguyen, but the storyline doesn't reflect it. I didn't expect the guy/girl scenes in this one to be worth watching, and so I wasn't at all disappointed with those. But where director McKendrick really dropped the ball was with the two girl/girl scenes. Only two? Seriously? Most people I know dearly LOVE watching lesbian scenes, but when you get a director who isn't interested, it shows, and this was one of those instances. Blonde amazon-warrior Jazy Berlin goes home with cute little Christine Nguyen, but when it comes time for those two to have sex, it falls flat. Jazy pushes the dark-haired girl down onto the couch, which at least had a bit of a dominant/submissive feel about it, but then they both kind of tentatively go at it, with neither woman playing even the slightest bit of attention to the other's gorgeous behind! A talented and/or creative director would have made it hot. This wasn't hot! The scene with red-haired amazon Erika Jordan and black girl Misty Stone was even worse. They just begin having sex because they're both in the same locker room together. It's like director McKendrick just wasn't interested. He tried much harder with the guy/girl scenes, but I fast-forwarded through all of them. Where are the writers/directors out there who appreciate girl/girl scenes? Notice that there are no names of men on the DVD box cover? Somebody needs to explain why that is to director Dean McKendrick.

history.title: Sinister
history.review_title: Creepy, scary movie that, in the end, made no sense!
history.text: I'm a huge fan of "The Ring," and because of this, somebody recommended "Sinister" to me. But they're not the same. Not even close. This one simply wasn't entertaining. It was certainly disturbing in parts and even included a few brief scary moments, but the overall story here was WEAK. A certain demonic figure named "Mr. Boogie" apparently incites children to commit horrific murders of their family members. Why? Who knows? It just happens. A crime-writer tries to figure it out, but gets nowhere, aside from viewing several creepy film clips that have been provided for him by forces beyond our control. When it was all over, I thought to myself: "Well, that was certainly a waste of time!"

history.title: The Shannara Chronicles: Season 1
history.text: Season one is loosely based on "The Elfstones of Shannara," book, and I use the words loosely-based because they have made wholesale changes to the plot. In this version, to become a member of the "Chosen" you have to finish near the top of a brutal type of athletic obstacle-course, whereas in the book the Ellcrys (the guardian tree that protects the elves from demons) selects each Chosen simply by touching them with one of her branches. In this version, Amberle & Eretria hate each-other (at least at the start), whereas in the book there was very little rancor between them, ever. This version adds a bizarre old man and a little girl at the Pykon ruins, who never existed in the book (and add nothing to the overall story). They also add an old-west town (named "Utopia") equipped with electric lights, a projector that shows "Star Trek" (no, I am serious), and dance-music played on a turntable to complete a nightclub-like atmosphere where the townsfolk of Utopia can party together. Needless to say, the book has NONE of that! The book DOES include an evil witch named Mallenroh (absent here), and the Amberle in the television series takes her sweet time getting around to restoring the Ellcrys, while her people are being slaughtered all around her! In other words, it's a deeply-flawed-yet-fun series to watch. Just don't expect it to faithfully stick to the novel on which it's based!

WHY, for example, does somebody walk away from the pack, but when they call out his name seconds later he refuses to answer, even though he can still hear them? Answer: it's so they can add some meaningless tension that ceases to mean anything after it happens the eighth or ninth time! And, of course, the evil guy is able to take over the minds of people, meaning that ANYBODY can be evil. It all got too stupid by the end. Terrible writers have no business making films!

history.text: To me it seemed like a whole lot of emotional religious blather surrounding one scientific fact (at least we believe they are facts) about Kepler's mathematical principles being put into computer programs that allow us to recreate the movements of the stars and planets were at any given moment in history. That was the one takeaway I got from this. The rest was just annoying. Larson was an annoying presenter; if I had him teaching a class on any subject I would likely find him patronizing and egotistical to point of walking out of the class. I believe in God and the possibility of the virgin birth. I don't believe this film offered anything of substance.

history.review_title: Russian melodrama merges 5 Hallmark movies into one.
history.text: Music is melancholic and repetitive throughout; gets a little wearing after 20 minutes - hang on for another 2 and 1/2 hours and you're home. I enjoyed seeing the Russian countryside and styles of living - even though movies always upscale how someone on an average paycheck can afford to live. The acting was indeed good, as other reviewers said. My problem with it is that it's like 5 hallmark movies sewn together with Russian melodrama. Even when things are going well, the music is foreboding. How much foreboding can a viewer take? The best parts were where the lovely gray mare was included. And at least most of the characters ended up somewhat resolved into a better frame of mind.

history.review_title: " He said he had an amazingly fun time making this movie and getting in touch with ...

He said he had an amazingly fun time making this movie and getting in touch with his feminine side. I can see why. Being fully supportive of the LGBT community and absolutely loving drag queens and Patrick Swayze I had to give this movie a look and I'm glad I did. I laughed more than I have in months but there is a lot more to the story than just three men dressing up and pretending to be divas. It's hard for people to get accepted for being who they truly are and want to be and no matter ever you go, there'll always be someone who will not accept you simply because of this or that. This movie can be very uplifting for people like that. It'll even melt your heart and put a tear in your eye in some scenes. 5 stars!

history.review_title: underrrated and very versatile actor so he played an amazingly good Jeff Bauman
history.text: Under unfortunate circumstances I did not get to see this movie in theater because it was only playing in “select” movie theaters as I was told, so I was pleasantly surprised to see it on Amazon Video yesterday. Jake Gyllenhaal is a phenomenal, underrrated and very versatile actor so he played an amazingly good Jeff Bauman. I cannot, however, understand the need for as much vulgarity as was used in this film. I’m not sure if it’s just true to real life or what, but the “f” word is used a profound amount of times. Other than that, this is a very captivating and heartwrenching catch on the real story and the main focal point of this movie is set AFTER the bombing to show what life was like for Jeff - which was very tear jerking at times. But in the end it can truly be a lesson for those of us who take life and all of the little things we have for granted - not to mention the good and evil that surrounds us. I definitely recommend this movie!

Over a decade ago I went to High School with a boy who dressed up like Eric Draven on a normal basis. My clothing and lifestyle (goth) were questionable to most from the outside looking in and despite regrettably not having seen The Crow when my friend would take bathroom breaks at school just to apply his Eric Draven look - it was years later that I realized why. And looking back, I wish I’d have paid more attention to his love for Eric and The Crow because this old friend of mine deserved praise for the excellent job at portraying him that he did. This film certainly uses some differences than the graphic novel but it doesn’t take away from the perfection or ability to appreciate the differentiations that the movie crew decided to use when planning and filming the movie. It’s a dark movie that someone with a truly deep personality can appreciate. At times the script is laughable (and not in a comedic way, but a way that will make you say “did they really just say that?”) but with such a strong backbone to the story and factoring in the few instances in real life that occurred to inspire this story I can overlook the flaws and not flinch when rating this movie a full 5 stars. Brandon Lee passed away while this film was still in production but I imagine he would’ve been proud. I wish he were still here and had retained the chance that he deserved to go on as a young, upcoming and talented actor as well as achievements he would’ve made in his own personal life. If you’ve yet to see this movie I fully encourage it. It’s one I’ll always kick myself over for not having seen it earlier in my younger years.

history.review_title: ... (and misconception) that it was going to be just like half of the other remakes out there - pointless ...
history.text: I went into this movie with the preconception (and misconception) that it was going to be just like half of the other remakes out there - pointless and unnecessary amongst other choice negative words. I'm the type of person who likes to keep an open mind but when I first saw the trailer for Jumanji (2017) all I could think was that Robin Williams would be rolling over in his grave at how cheesy this movie looked and how forced the short trailer really was. I was undoubtedly wrong. Seeing this movie in theater was merely because it was by invitation from my brother to get out of the house, plus he'd offered to pay. 20 minutes into the film is when the true action really began and it didn't stop until the ending credits began rolling. It's an absolutely well put together movie with a mix of well known and not so well known actors but it truly panned out. There is an extremely high amount of funny parts in this movie but not to the point that it overwhelmed the actual plot or purpose to the movie. And the small homage they paid to Robin Williams in the middle of the movie I was appreciative of. I can't say enough good things about this movie other than you should see it!

history.review_title: I love period pieces and am willing to give many movies ...
history.text: I’ve been in the mood to watch a bunch of Billy Zane films lately and this is one I hadn’t made it to yet up until yesterday. I love period pieces and am willing to give many movies a chance, even if they seem like they’re not in my taste or (as stated above) simply because of someone’s role in them. From sources I’ve read and looked at, Billy Zane was said to be one of the main characters and leading roles (after Tilda) in this film. He was in a total of 5 minutes of this movie, lol. Either way, I managed to stick it out through this film and having not known of the existence of a book that supposedly inspired this movie. It was truly a tornado of confusion for me. I tried my best to understand what was going on but the plot line skipped all over the place and before I could register what had happened it skipped to the next part/chapter of the movie. 2 stars for Billy’s short performance and handsome good looks. 😊 I can’t politely rate the movie anything.
