history.review_title: Very good exposition of a new science
history.text: Very informed and comprehensive presentation of the neuron cluster that controls digestion, immunity, and a host of other bodily functions we could not live without. Of course, if you believe the Earth is flat, is 6,000 years old, or that evolution is a lie foisted on the world by evil scientists, just skip this. The filmmakers don't deserve a bad review because you are ill-informed.

history.title: The Founder
history.review_title: Its about business (not really McDonalds, so much)
history.text: I loved this movie because it tells the unvarnished truth about an American business empire, and makes sly commentary on business in general. Well acted, well filmed, with great story and empathetic characters. This is not really about McDonalds, per se'. Its about business. And Michael Keaton is at the top of his game. Watching him act is a pleasure.

history.title: Red Pill, The
history.text: Easily one of the best, most even- handed documentaries I have seen in fifty years of living. Journalists and other documentary makers could learn a great deal from how Cassie Jaye just let her interview subjects speak their mind and finish their thoughts. She didn't interrupt anyone which was elating in and of itself. We have become so used to journalists and film makers talking over their subject (especially the 60 Minutes crew, sadly) and directing the narrative that when you see someone who doesn't do it, you become invested in what the subjects are actually saying. And in letting her subjects speak, she at once gives them enough rope to hang themselves, or gives them enough latitude to convey salient meaning. She also does a very good job of honest analysis of the information along the way, giving the viewer some personal perspective which is helpful.

history.review_title: Wish I had read the reviews before watching...
history.text: Very slow and drawn out, because the case is unsolved, the police were absolutely bumbling, no facts are presented, and the entire story is quiet guitar music behind interviews with the relatives and friends of the victims. Its all just emotional impressions of five people lost. The filmmakers made no attempt to address how the victims were killed, the condition of the bodies, what evidence was available --- nothing.
Oh brother...The Amazon description states that this as, "an authentic documentary". I have an authentic piece of ocean-front property in Florida I'd like to sell you too.

history.review_title: More entertaining than just staring out the window, but not by much
history.text: Nothing happens in this movie. Time does move forward, just like in our world. But other than that, nope. The characters seem to be intentionally monotone, one dimensional projections of people (except for the childlike girlfriend). The "poetry" is ... well, try this: write down whatever random thoughts you have while washing the dishes or brushing your teeth. Congratulations - you've written poetry. To be fair, the cinematography is gorgeous. New Jersey never looked so good.
Its Dirty Harry. Nuff said.

history.review_title: Interesting to learn that Wakefield has never been against infant vaccinations
history.text: Very interesting to learn that Wakefield never in any way suggested a cessation of infant vaccinations. Due to an unmistakable statistical correlation between administration of the MMR vaccine (measles, mumps, rubella) and a verifiable dramatic rise in the onset of autism (from 1 in 10,000 30 years ago to 1 in 50 now), he and his superiors recommended 1) that the vaccinations be administered as three separate inoculations instead of the single MMR while more testing and research could be done, and 2) that the data suggested that it would be safer if the triple inoculation be postponed from 15 months to 3 years of age. The UK gov't's answer to this was to ban all single inoculations. That is verifiable historical fact. They did this. Look it up. There is also incontrovertible truth that the US CDC purposely altered research data to suggest no tenable link between autism and the MMR inoculation. There seems to be quite a bit of half-truths and misinformation the other side is shouting towards these people. Just read some of the comments about the movie and "anti-vaxxers": "Anti-vaxxers are stupid, stupid, stupid, stupid, stupid, stupid" (a real review of this movie, right here on Amazon). Watch the film, do some additional research, and make up your own mind.

Its almost impossible to review this movie in any depth without spoilers. But I'll give it a shot. For instance: if you've ever suffered through the experience of having a clingy, selfish, psychopath friend who is a habitual line-stepper and requires you to solve their problems and make them happy, this movie will give you awful flashbacks. There are parts that are hard to watch because of that. And the writer doesn't give you anyone to empathize with: pretty much all the main characters have serious flaws. However it does make you think in terms of bad and good, and how 90% of everything anyone does is some shade of gray. Its fairly obvious that this film was made on a budget, but for the most part the acting is well done and cinematography sufficient to help you suspend disbelief for and hour 42. The writing really stands out. An original idea that could easily happen in real life. For that matter, it probably has...

history.review_title: Ignore the bad reviews; this is a fantastic flick
history.text: Exceptional movie that is heartfelt, thoughtful, and creative in how it avoids Hollywood formula to delve into the finer aspects of the human psyche. It involves time travel, yes, but only as a tool to facilitate the story arc and make the viewer ask, How well do you know yourself? I loved this flick.

targets.title: We Need to Talk About Kevin

history.title: Baywatch
history.review_title: A lame resurrection of an old TV favorite
history.text: Well, I knew what I was getting myself in for, so I can’t be too smug about this reimagined popular TV series that ran from 1989 to 2001. The biggest problem is that the film seems to swing too far in the direction of an earnest “police” drama then back to the campy silliness that was most likely the target. The writers even go so far as to bring up the absurdity of a lifeguard doing police undercover work, but they do it anyway. Speaking of the writers (there are 5!) they get a couple things right. Mitch (Dwayne Johnson) use of various TV, musical groups and movie names he calls the Ryan Lochte-like Olympic swimmer Matt Brody (a ripped Zac Efron). Names like “One Direction” and “High School Musical.” Brody says to Mitch, he’ll correct the error of his ways, if Mitch will call him by his real name. Think that will ever happen? The other scene which is pretty funny is when Brody and Mitch break into the morgue to check out the cause of death of a councilman (Oscar Nunez). Mitch directs Brody to check the area between the ball sack and the anus for signs of foul play. It is one of two scenes of nudity in the film. The other is the backside of the one actor you would just as soon keep his pants on. But let’s face it, most people are going to watch this film for the physical appearance of the actors in very brief bathing suits. That is a success. The three females (Alexandra Daddario, Kelly Rohrbach and Ilfenesh Hadera) are perfect specimens of the gender. Toss in Priyanka Chopra as the bad girl and you have a pretty picture. And that is complemented by Efron and “The Rock.” The guy with the bare butt scene is poor Jon Bass who plays the other lifeguard who made the team based on his determination says Mitch. Johnson is always fun to watch and his chemistry with Efron is very good. The acting? Well, hopefully everyone got paid. The script and the editing is very poor. There are several scenes that go back and forth between camera angles and the people aren’t even in the same position. The jiggle factor is high, so there is that. Bikinis galore and everyone on the beach looks good in them. Otherwise this is a pretty lame resurrection of an old favorite.

history.title: The Room
history.review_title: 1 1/2 stars for a terrible movie, as bad as it gets, and a cult classic that should be seen by everyone.
history.text: Possible spoilers. This is one of those movies that is entertaining, but probably not in the way the filmmaker(s) wanted. A new movie is coming out soon called “The Disaster Artist” and features the making of this movie and its star, director, writer and producer Tommy Wiseau. Frankly I had not heard of it until recently but I got a copy on DVD and gave it a look. The plot, as it were, involves Johnny (Wiseau) who is some kind of banker (I think) who wears suits about 3 sizes too big. Wiseau has one of those accents that is hard to place. It would appear to be part Eastern European with a mix of Cajun. He sounds and looks as if he has a mouth full of marbles. Johnny has been with Lisa (Juliette Danielle) for 6 years and is looking forward to getting married soon. With the film barely underway, the pair engage in a very long “love” scene in their San Francisco apartment. But not before an 18 year old Denny (Philip Haldiman) who is “like-a-son” to Johnny comes in to watch. He’s in love with Lisa too. He’s shoed away like a pet dog and our couple get back to business. You’ll see this scene recreated again later in the film using the same footage as near as I could tell. It turns out that Lisa isn’t in love with Johnny anymore much to her mother’s (Carolyn Minnott) regret. Mom likes Johnny and she wants her daughter to marry him regardless of the fact that Lisa now loves Mark (Greg Sestero), Johnny’s best friend who also lives in the building. So does Denny and probably mom since she pops in often for no reason other than to deliver a few lines. The movie is incoherent in spite of its simplicity. Characters show up with no explanation or idea of who they are. We get scenes that just appear out of nowhere. Probably the best is when Johnny, Denny, Mark and Peter (Kyle Vogt) appear in an alley in tuxedos and start tossing a football around. Peter is evidently a psychologist and another of Johnny’s friends. Based on the scene, it appears to be the first time they’ve ever seen a football…or any ball for that matter. It’s hilarious. It is no surprise that I didn’t know any of the actors and it appears that none have made much of a career since the film’s release. The acting is close to horrible by all concerned but Wiseau’s script doesn’t help. His performance will have everyone laughing every time he opens his mouth, or enters a room, or just reacts. Just Wow! I’ve seen many of the classic clunkers including Troll 2, Plan 9 from Outer Space (and most of Ed Woods’ films), all the Sharknadoes and Showgirls to name a few. Without question this is the worst I’ve ever seen, but damn I had a good time. See it with as many people as you can.

history.title: Girls Trip [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: 3 1/2 stars for a raunchy, fun trip
history.text: Possible spoilers. This is another of those purposely raunchy movies made with women in the central roles. It used to be the sole domain of the boys, but no more. Earlier this summer we had “Rough Night,” a similarly themed film. This trip features Regina Hall as Ryan Pierce who along with her husband, Stewart (Mike Colter), are on the verge of creating a social juggernaut based on their book, “You Can Have It All” (or something to that effect). About to strike it rich, Ryan and Stewart get invited to the Essence Music Festival in New Orleans (where else?). They are to meet with a potential financial supporter that would land them a long term deal. Ryan decides it would be a good opportunity to get the old gang back together (Stewart will come later) for a fun few days around her meeting. The old gang consists of Sasha (Queen Latifah) a one-time college friend and potential business partner that never was. Lisa (Jada Pinkett Smith) is a single mother who has put romance on the back burner. Finally Dina (Tiffany Haddish) seems to be just a gal they keep around for laughs (her words). The plot, as it is, involves the ladies getting into a lot of trouble with alcohol, drugs and sexual desires key elements. Oh, there is the overriding story of how Ryan just might not “have it all” after all. The best reason to see this film – assuming you can handle the nudity, language, sex and raunchy behavior – is Tiffany Haddish. She adds the spark needed in films like this and has the one laugh-out-loud moment when she teaches Lisa how to employ a grapefruit during sex. The rest of the movie is smile-worthy and highly predictable. Still the girls trip was a lot of fun for this guy.

history.title: Roman J. Israel, Esq.
history.review_title: 3 1/2 stars for a good film and a great performance by Denzel Washington
history.text: Theater review. Possible spoilers. This is director Dan Gilroy’s sophomore effort coming after the excellent “Nightcrawler” from 2014. It features Denzel Washington in one of his best performances. Washington plays a behind-the-scenes lawyer who works for a well-known icon specializing in low budget cases. The small 3-person firm, deeply in debt, falls into chaos when the head of the firm has a heart attack. We never see him other than hooked up to tubes in a hospital room. Washington’s Israel is something of a legal savant. He’s memorized the entire Los Angeles city code down to sub-paragraphs of sub-paragraphs and has primarily prepared strategies for his boss. He rarely appears in court and when he does we see why. He’s a socially uncomfortable and has a tendency to ramble on philosophically. When the family decides to dissolve the firm, Israel is in a bit of a lurch, financially and otherwise. Israel approaches a small charitable legal defense organization whose primary operative is Maya Alston (Carmen Ejogo). While this is probably a good fit for Israel, there is no pay. He later accepts a job at the firm led by George Pierce (Colin Farrell) who is in charge of shutting down Israel’s former office. But Israel clearly doesn’t fit in with the busy, profit-focused firm. Still Pierce sees something in Israel and gives him several opportunities including pro-bono cases. The story takes a wrong turn when Israel is assigned a case involving a 17-year old boy who was hanging with an older man who held up a convenience store. The clerk is killed but only the boy is caught. Israel makes some ethical and moral errors that seem out of character. I had a hard time swallowing this plot point. Still, there is no denying the great work Washington puts in here. His character is something very different from what he’s done before and should be recognized. His performance alone makes the film worthwhile. It is about 70% very good and 30% just OK.

history.review_title: 4 1/2 stars for a near masterpiece as the saga continues
history.text: Theater review. Possible spoilers. Under J. J. Abrams’ direction, “The Force Awakens” (2015) was the perfect reboot to get this franchise back underway. This second episode of the new trilogy puts Rian Johnson (“Looper”) at the helm along with writing responsibilities. He doesn’t disappoint. The story picks up where it ended in “The Force Awakens.” Rey (Daisy Ridley) has been sent by Leia (Carrie Fisher in her final performance) to retrieve her brother, Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill, never better) from his self-imposed exile on a mountainous island. One without the benefits of sun and sandy beaches. Luke isn’t interested as far as helping the Resistance against the First Order. He sees no future and is deeply disillusioned, about what we’re not sure but will find out later. After a couple days of reluctantly showing Rey a few light-sabre maneuvers, she leaves with Chewy (Joonas Suotamo) and his new friend, a Porg leaving Luke behind. I was a little worried about the intro of this new cutie pie to the series. I was never a fan of the Ewoks in the earlier adventures. Thankfully, they don’t contribute or take away much which is also something you can say about Chewbacca in this episode. They do, however contribute to one of the funnier scenes in the film which leads to another point. Johnson has several scenes that involve humor including some great one-liners. Don’t get me wrong this isn’t a funny film, far from it. It mixes some state-of-the-art actions sequences and a handful of carefully plotted missions carried out by the film’s stars. Oscar Isaac returns as Poe Dameron, a rebel within the rebellion. John Byega returns as Finn who gets paired up with newcomer, Rose Tico (Kelly Marie Tran) to steal a tracking code with help from a character called DJ (Benicio Del Toro). Purple haired Vice Admiral Holdo (Laura Dern) has to take over from a comatose Leia and surprises everyone with her heroics. Some of the best scenes are between Rey and Kylo Ren (Adam Driver) who you might remember have a telepathic connection. The best being when Kylo brings Rey before his master, the evil Snoke (Andy Serkis). I will admit to being a bit miffed that we don’t learn much about Snoke and how he came to be. A nice surprise, however is how we see how characters struggle with “The Force” and “The Dark Side.” Remember the power struggle between Kylo and General Hux (Domhnall Gleeson) in the earlier film? Resolved. Quibbles? Sure. The film is long at 2 ½ hours. Cuts could have been made perhaps during the “casino” scenes which provides some action fun, but don’t add much to the story. Carrie Fisher’s final performance is very good but Johnson saddled her with an outrageous scene and a send-off that could have been better. While those issues may just be my own, they keep the film from perfection.

history.title: Jumanji
history.review_title: A good story whose focus is ambivalent
history.text: Possible spoilers. There’s a new Jumanji movie coming out in a few days starring “The Rock” Johnson, Jack Black and others. Although I have this original on DVD, I never took the time to watch it. Until now. The film was directed by Joe Johnston (“Captain America: The First Avenger”) and starred the late Robin Williams as Alan Parrish. I was also curious to see Kirsten Dunst as 13 year old Judy Shepherd. A year after her well-talked about appearance in “Interview with the Vampire.” The film opens in 1869 New Hampshire with a Jumanji board game being buried with an ominous voice over of a character stating “God help anyone who digs this up.” A quick jump 100 years later and a bullied 13-year old Alan (Adam Hann-Byrd) is upset that his wealthy dad, Sam (Jonathan Hyde) plans on sending Alan to a famous private school. Alan decides he’s leaving home, so packs his suitcase with essentials (a loaf of bread, peanut butter) and heads out. He stops near an excavation site and finds an old chest which contains the Jumanji game. He decides to go back home and see what’s what. His friend Sarah (Laura Bell Bundy) comes over and they decide to play the game. Both are surprised that with a roll of the dice, the pieces move by themselves and bring a message magically as if in a flat crystal ball. With the first roll, the house is invaded by huge bats. One of the rules of the game is that you have to continue it to the end in order for everything to go back as it was. Well young Sarah doesn’t want to play anymore, so Alan is swept into the game board as Sarah flees the bats. The story jumps 26 years and Nora Shepherd (Bebe Neuwirth) has bought the old house that belonged to the wealthy Parrish family. She is the aunt of Judy and her younger brother, Peter (Bradley Pierce). Never completely explained, Judy and Peter’s parents are dead. The youngsters find the old board-game in the attic and of course decide to give it a whirl. The first role of the dice brings giant mosquitos. And Robin Williams as the older Alan, now freed from inside the game which is evidently a jungle, although we never go there. Alan, Peter and Judy decide they need to finish the game for things to get back to normal. But first want to see if they can find Alan’s old friend, Sarah now played by Bonnie Hunt. It seems the 26 years since Alan disappeared haven’t been good ones for her either. When asked about what happened to Alan at the time, she told the truth and has been ostracized ever since. So now they are back to the game and with each roll they get more problem invaders like violent monkeys, spiders, a lion, car-crushing vines and a lunatic hunter named Van Pelt (Hyde again) whose only job is to kill Alan. No explanation given. The movie actually had me going early on but things changed for the worse. It starts out as a tension based fantasy and devolves into a slapstick comedy with occasional frightening sequences that come quickly and exit just as quickly into thin air. Well except for the monkeys who can now drive cars and motorcycles. The worst of these scenes involves a policeman played by David Alan Grier. He and his patrol car are often the brunt of what are calculated focuses of the humor. I will make another point. I thought the special effects were pretty bad even for 1995. The film seems to fall into a black hole in terms of its intended audiences. It’s rated PG but seems a bit too scary for little kids and maybe just a bit too stupid for older kids. A good story that seems to lose its way.

history.title: The Bad Batch
history.review_title: 3 1/2 stars for Ms. Amipour's sophomore effort. More please.
history.text: Possible spoilers. One of my favorite movies from 2015 (U.S. release) was an Iranian vampire western called “A Girl Walks Home Alone at Night.” It was written and directed by Ana Lily Amipour, a British born American and her first feature film. The film is dark (literally shot in black and white), funny, poetic, romantic and featured a killer soundtrack. Her second film while still dark (figuratively) is a much different landscape. It is set in the bright sun of the Texas desert (shot in California) but still features a bit of humor and romance and still has a killer soundtrack. The film opens in the near-future – think Mad Max setting but in Texas – and the powers that are in charge release undesirables, a loose term that seems to include the undocumented, the mentally handicapped and others who don’t “fit” into society, into the barren desert. A young woman named Arlen (Suki Waterhouse) is one of those people, although we’re never told of what makes her unfit. Given a jug of water off she goes, not quite sure of what to expect. Certainly not a colony of cannibalistic body builders. She soon learns that she will become dinner. She leaves an arm and a leg but manages to escape back into the desert creatively using a skateboard as a getaway vehicle. Near death, she is found by a grizzled hermit (an unrecognizable Jim Carrey) and taken to a town called Comfort which doesn’t condone cannibalism. A few months later she is fitted with an artificial leg which allows her to amble around town. The town is run by a cult-like leader called The Dream (Keanu Reeves) who lives in comparative luxury surrounded by a score of lovelies, most of whom are pregnant, but bare automatic rifles. The Dream’s claim to fame seems to be relative tranquility and flushing toilets. Back in cannibal town, Miami Man (Jason Momoa) lives with the mother (Yolonda Ross) of their 10-year old girl (Jayda Fink). Mom and Honey (Fink) go exploring the nearest radioactive dump for useful stuff and mom is seriously injured. Arlen happens to be out for a stroll and comes across the pair. Armed with a 6-shooter Arlen kills the mom which poses the question, why. Either she was just pissed off that mom was one of the cannibals or perhaps just had an itchy trigger finger. We’re not sure. In any case, Arlen returns to Comfort with Honey in tow. Miami Man, wondering where his family is, sets out on a scooter to find them. He comes across the hermit who trades him their whereabouts for a picture of him. It turns out Miami Man is a bit of an artist. Thankfully Momoa doesn’t have many lines because he clearly struggles with his Cuban accent…and so do we. Eventually Miami Man meets up with Arlen in the desert (she likes to wander bad leg and all). With little regard as to what happened to mom, Miami Man wants Arlen to find his daughter for him. Unfortunately young Honey is in the hands of The Dream and Arlen will have to make some tough decisions. The film features Giovanni Ribisi as a mentally disturbed character called The Screamer and an uncredited Diego Luna as Jimmy the DJ in small roles. The movie has too many head-scratchers to make it all make sense and the pacing and length could be improved. At the same time, the movie has a great look, has some modern cultural themes and moves the needle further for Ms. Amirpour. I want to see more.

history.title: All The Money In The World
history.review_title: 4 1/2 stars for a well-crafted thriller primed for awards.
history.text: Theater review. Possible spoilers. Unless you’ve been living in a cave, you probably have heard about the recent publication of improprieties of actor Kevin Spacy over the years. This terrific Ridley Scott film had Spacy in a key role as J. Paul Getty, the 80-year old oil baron. Scott made a decision to replace Spacy with 88-year old actor, Christopher Plummer (“Beginners”) and still release the film by Christmas. The film had already been completed and was in the editing stages but Scott felt it important to make the changes. With a reported shooting schedule of 4 days to reshoot Plummer’s scenes he managed to open the film on time. Perhaps most remarkable is that Plummer’s performance may be the highlight of the film. Most surprising to me is that there are a lot of scenes not just a handful! The film is based on the factual kidnapping in 1973 of Getty’s 16-year old grandson, Paul (Charlie Plummer, no relation). The senior Getty was living in London at the time and his alcoholic son JP II (Andrew Buchan) was divorced from Gail (Michelle Williams) who had custody of the children. We get a brief flashback to an earlier time when II and Gail were living in the U. S. and II was having a hard time getting a job. Estranged from his father, he finally writes and asks him for a job. Senior Getty wants II and his family to meet him in Rome. He says he has a job waiting. Philandering, alcohol and drugs precludes the divorce. Gail agrees to no alimony or settlement, just child support. Back to the present, young Paul is kidnapped off the streets of Rome and whisked to the countryside where the kidnappers demand $17 million from Gail who they assume has the money or can get it from her former father-in-law. Well, Gail is broke and grandpa, who is the richest man in the world and probably the richest man in the history of the world refuses to pay anything. Instead he uses his head of security, Fletcher Chase (Mark Wahlberg) to track down the kidnappers and keep Gail under wraps. But Gail is no shrinking violet and confronts the old man as best she can. I kept my eyes peeled for signs of disconnect from the movie and the new scenes involving Plummer. I could only see one possible case. When Gail, II and the kiddies (3 or 4) first meet grandpa, they mysteriously disappear with only Gail, II and Paul in the scene. Otherwise, it was a seamless edit. The film certainly has the capitalistic theme of the pompous old man who would pay a million dollars for an artifact but nothing for ransom for his flesh and blood. But the film really is a procedural thriller. The police, Gail and Chase do their best to track down the kidnapped boy. The scenes with Paul and the lead kidnapper are very good. Cinquanta (Romain Duris) keeps the boy as safe as he can, but eventually decides to “sell” the boy to other bad guys as the negotiations drag on for months. Both Duris and young Plummer are terrific. I would expect Christopher Plummer and perhaps Michelle Williams to get some attention with Oscar nominations coming up. The film is tightly shot, perfectly performed and highly entertaining. Highly recommended.

history.title: The Shape of Water
history.review_title: Guillermo del Toro's latest creature feature is a good one, flush with "R" rated romance.
history.text: Theater review. Possible spoilers. While watching this film in a sparsely populated multiplex theater, a few people began to walk out midway through the movie. I’ve seen this before and I always find myself guessing why. I mean what were they expecting? My guess with this film is that it is a tale of fantasy. One involving romance with a humanoid-like creature but clearly not human. I’m sure everyone knows of the numerous iterations of “Beauty and the Beast” but don’t get upset. Maybe the difference is that this film is pretty graphic, not only with the brutality of beast’s captivity but of the bold sexual context. Guillermo del Toro’s beast this time is a South American river creature considered a god by the local population. The creature is played by Doug Jones and resembles another character created by del Toro and played by Jones in “Hellboy II.” He has a dual lung composition which allows him to spend time out of water, but he prefers being in it. The web-handed (and footed) creature was captured by Richard Strickland (Michael Shannon in another great performance), an instrument of the U. S. government. It’s 1962 and the military believes there may be some benefit to studying the creature and its potential powers. The large facility where the creature is kept includes a cleaning crew. One of the cleaning ladies is Elisa Esposito (an Oscar-worthy performance by Sally Hawkins) who can hear but cannot speak due to some mysterious mishap many years earlier. Her best friend and fellow cleaner is Zelda Fuller (Octavia Spencer) provides plenty of dialog to offset Elisa’s mute. Elisa, while not speaking still communicates fully using facial gestures and her own form of sign language. Michael Stuhlbarg plays Dr. Hoffstetler, the primary scientist responsible for studying the creature. Sides are quickly set as Strickland who is a bully, a thug and a sexual predator throws his weight around using a cattle prod as his reinforcement. Hoffstetler, like most movie scientists is more interested in studying the creature not torturing him. He has other secrets that will come into play later. Elisa lives over a movie theater and her friend and neighbor is a gay man named Giles (Richard Jenkins) who like Elisa is love-starved and struggles to make ends meet as an artist for an advertising firm. Elisa is curious more than anything about the captive creature and slowly begins to approach him when he’s in his water tank, constrained around the neck. The fact that the two beings must communicate non-verbally makes it all seem to make sense. The creature, while not handsome by human sensibilities, has a certain character doesn’t make him repulsive. Over time, the two become close. When it becomes clear the creature will be killed and dissected, Elisa and her friends chart a plan to free him. Screenwriting chores are from del Toro and Vanessa Taylor. Del Toro has admitted he based the story on his love of the movie “Creature from the Black Lagoon” which he first saw as a 6-year old. It’s one of my favorite movies too. Certainly the resemblance between the creatures in the films differ primarily from the advanced costume designs of today. I was a bit puzzled by the amount of time Elisa had to keep the creature under wraps before freeing him back into the water. Under the circumstances it seemed odd, not to mention dangerous. Still, I guess it allows time for the unusual heightening of the romantic angle. There is another scene in the film which might make some people slap their forehead in bewilderment, but like the whole movie, just go with it. After all it’s a fairy tale for grown-ups and a sensitive one at that. While del Toro’s imagination is primarily responsible for it all, it is Hawkins who makes it work. Recommended…for most people.

history.title: Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle [DVD]
history.text: Theater review. Possible spoilers. I only recently watched the original 1995 “Jumanji” and was underwhelmed, recognizing that the movie is beloved by many. In that movie, all the action takes place in the present day New Hampshire. In this reboot, the action takes place in the magical jungle of the game itself. The only reference to the older movie is a brief scene where the Alan Parrish character is “remembered” by Alex (singer Nick Jonas) who was sucked into the game 20-years earlier. We see this in an opening scene. The primary focus of this film centers around 4 high school students who all end up in detention at the same time. Spencer (Alex Wolff) is a geeky loner who writes term papers for the football star, Fridge (Ser’Darious Blain). They get caught. Bethany (Madison Iseman) is the hottie who can’t turn off her smart phone and Martha (Morgan Turner) refuses to participate in gym class. While stewing in a dingy room after school, they find the Jumanji game. Spencer, naturally a gamer, hooks it up (yep, updated to an electronic game) to a TV and they all decide to play. Before they play they must choose an avatar and before you know it, they get sucked into the game ending up in the land that is Jumanji. What makes this film come to life is that the real life characters arrive in the bodies of their avatar. Whimpy Spencer becomes an Indiana Jones type but with a very big body with very big muscles (Duane Johnson). Hulky Fridge is a zoologist in the body of diminutive Kevin Hart. Wallflower Martha becomes a kick-ass martial arts Lara Croft-type complete with the short shorts and bare midriff. Best of all is sexpot Bethany becomes cartographer in the body of Jack Black. Hart is very funny and his bits with Johnson are terrific, but he really doesn’t do much in terms of replicating the identity of his bruising fullback. Black has some of the best lines and scenes as you might imagine. A laugh out loud moment comes when Bethany has to urinate using Black’s body. So what does this quartet have to do to get back home and back to their real bodies? Nigel (Rhys Darby) is kind of their guide and tells them they must retrieve the softball sized emerald stone from the local evil power monger, Van Pelt (Bobby Cannavale) and return it to its proper place with a giant Jaguar statue high in the mountains. The problem of course is Van Pelt who has the stone. He seems to have control of all the animals, many of which are sent after our heroes. The movie is quick moving and has some decent if not exceptional, special effects. The action is pretty good as well and of course there is some heightened awareness of social improvement for each character. Certainly the theme of working together comes into play. Romance? Sure. Spencer and Martha have an innocent “thing.” Better is Bethany (Black) oogling both Spencer and Alex (Jonas). There are plenty of very funny scenes and that is the reason you will want to see this movie. Recommended.

history.title: Dark Shadows: The Complete Original Series (Deluxe Edition)
history.text: I have been considering buying this for months but the price was daunting. However it was the Amazon deal of the day this week at a considerable discount ($279), so I finally pulled the trigger. I was still a little leery about spending so much money until the set arrived. I was a bit concerned after reading some of the reviews about damage during shaping, but it was very well packed in a thick, stiff box conformed to the coffin shape. That box was packed by Amazon in a larger box and well cushioned with packing material. The coffin itself was further protected in a plastic bag. So mine was in perfect shape. The coffin is quite nice and well constructed of sturdy cardboard with metal hinges. It is larger, heavier and more solid than I expected. The DVDs are in perfect shape and none had come loose during shipping. I have only watched the first 5 episodes, but the quality is better than I expected for such an old show shot on videotape. The production values (camera, lighting, music, etc) are also better than I expected. I am hooked. To sum up, I don't regret this purchase at all. It is well worth the price I paid and I have probably a year or more worth of material to watch. If you are leery of the price, keep an eye on the amazon deal, it will probably come up again.

history.title: Triangle [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: Great psychological horror film that requires a little thinking
history.text: This is a gem of a film that most people don't know about. I won't go into spoilers, but suffice to say it has a multi-layered plot and it takes some thinking after it's over to figure out what happened. The less you know going in the better. A second viewing is almost essential to really appreciate and enjoy it. There are clues and symbols cleverly scattered througout. The movie follows an internal logic and does indeed make sense. I think that the few one star reviews are from people who didn't get it or didn't like having to use their brains a little bit. The photography is good and the performances are mostly good. I have seen this film 3 times now and have noticed something new each time. Highly recommended for people who are sick of brainless, formulaic hollywood horror films.

history.review_title: Occasionally fun but ultimately too derivative and unsatisfying
history.text: I had high hopes for this movie but was disappointed. There is a smattering of cleverness, but it is diminished by the filmmakers need to constantly show just how amazingly clever and hip they are. Some of the humor is really lame and juvenile (and homophobic, in 2013, just eye-rollingly stupid). The heroes are so aloof, sarcastic and unconcerned with anyone or anything going on around them that they become completely unlikable. It's one thing to have a reluctant hero, but these guys are just self-absorbed douchebags. By the time we get to the wink-wink ending where they smugly swagger away from helping the future world (or whatever it is) because they are bored with saving the world and would rather play basketball (or something) I was completely disconnected. This kind of ironic/cynical thing MIGHT have been fresh and clever about 20 years ago, but now it plays as really stale. That is the problem with most of the movie, it just recycles and regurgitates what was innovative circa early 90s and has nothing new or original to contribute. And then pats itself on the back constantly for how amazingly clever it thinks it is. The weirdness and quirkyness of the (nonsensical) plot is forced and self-conscious. Weird and quirky is now the cliche of independent films. Things are thrown in just to be weird, not because of an artistic intent or to advance the plot, but because it's now the norm. People keep comparing it to Naked Lunch, but that film was something new at the time. This is a faded photocopy of a photocopy of that movie. It's not that I don't "get" the movie. Like I said I was rooting for the movie and really wanted to like it, but it ultimately fails because its head is too far up its own rear.

history.title: Twin Peaks: The Entire Mystery [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: A Review of the Actual Product - It's A Fan's Dream Come True!
history.text: There have been so many people treating this section as a message board instead of reviews it's absurd. I have the set and have been watching it, so this is an actual REVIEW. PACKAGING The packaging is nicely done and good quality. However I prefer practical packaging and it takes a little effort to flip through and access the discs. There isn't a booklet listing all of the disc contents, which is a bit frustrating as you have to insert a disc to see which special features it contains. This is nitpicking because it looks very good and there is a neat little surprise after you flip through all of the discs. HD UPGRADE QUALITY All episodes of the TV show, including both versions of the pilot, have been meticulously scanned and remastered from the original negatives. People seem to forget that this show was finished in 1990 TV resolution. Thankfully it was shot on film and those film negatives could be used to create HD masters. It took considerable work and expense to upgrade these episodes to HD quality and DTS sound. While the Gold Box versions looked great, these transfers are much better, with 3 times the sharpness and more accurate and striking color. I am watching on a 100" screen and seeing textures and details I never noticed on the DVD. There is a much greater depth which pulls you even deeper into the world of Twin Peaks. Twin Peaks was the first show to be shot in a cinematic style, and it pays off big time on blu-ray. The shows are presented in their original 4x3 aspect ratio. I have noticed some shots in the first few episodes which were clearly not upgraded to HD, probably because they were part of a special effect. For example, when Laura's mom imagines Donna's face turning into Laura. They were brief moments and didn't detract much from the overall amazing presentation. However in the first episode of season two there is a long montage of superimposed shots while Cooper describes the details of Laura's murder. The whole sequence is noticeably not in HD and it stands out. It is quite distracting and a shame because it is such a crucial and visual scene. I can only guess the producers were unable to locate the original negative for those scenes. The sound is remixed and remastered in DTS-MA and is amazingly full ranged and detailed considering it was originally created for a 24 year old TV show. The music in particular sounds fantastic. Fire Walk With Me has not been previously available in HD in the US. The new transfer was scanned from the camera negative in 4k resolution and looks great. It has a very organic, natural film look with great depth and color. Sound is also DTS-MA and is excellent. I have a much greater appreciation for the film after watching it again in HD. There are still moments I don't like, but overall it is brilliant. The extras have all been upgraded to HD where possible and look great. Even the murky old Log Lady introductions (which is how the entire show looked back then) show a big improvement. I was thrilled to see that the recaps and previews for each episode have been included in HD. There are also some ABC promos. That really takes me back to watching it on ABC so many years ago. THE MISSING PIECES This is the biggest selling point of the set and for good reason. When Fire Walk with Me was released in 1992, many fans (myself included) were sorely disappointed when many favorite characters were not seen in the film. This frustration only increased when it was discovered that many of them were in fact filmed, but cut from the movie. Over the years these deleted scenes have become legendary, with entire websites devoted to drafts of scripts and rare photos from these scenes. In the era of DVD extra features, fans petitioned to get the deleted scenes released. However, there was a tangle of legal rights which prevented this from happening. Complicating matters was the fact that David Lynch refused to include the scenes in their rough, unfinished state. It would take considerable funding to complete them to Lynch's specifications. After years of trying, it was finally announced that negotiations were at a standstill and the scenes would not be released. That is why they have never been included before. I don't know exactly how it happened, but somehow the parties involved finally came to an agreement and funding was provided to allow Lynch to finally finish the scenes. Fans who have followed this saga for 22 years know how amazingly lucky we are to finally have 90 minutes of this legendary footage in full HD quality and DTS sound. Lynch presents the Missing Pieces as it's own movie type experience and they play as a series of vaguely connected vignettes. It doesn't make much sense if you haven't seen FWWM recently, so a fresh viewing first might be a good idea. And how are the scenes after all of these years? Do they live up to the hype? The answer is a definite YES. There is some amazing stuff here which Twin Peaks fans will love. There are both small character moments and big mind blowing moments. And about 5 minutes which take place AFTER the Season Two finale. You will find out what happens to Annie and get a further glimpse into what might have been with the evil Cooper if there was a season three. It's great stuff and I am still kind of amazed we are finally getting to see it. And in such great quality. I have not encountered audio sync issues as some have reported. EXTRAS In addition to the Missing Pieces, there are several new extras created for this set. I haven't watched them all yet, but I did watch Between Two Worlds, which has 2 parts. The first is a haunting and surreal conversation with the Palmer family and David Lynch. This is followed by a more casual conversation with the actors who portrayed them. Very entertaining and very Lynchian. The Atmospherics are trippy short music videos, each with a Twin Peaks theme and footage from the episodes and movie. There are several previously unreleased deleted scenes and outtakes from the show on Disc Four. There are 2 features on the making of FWWM, which I haven't watched yet. Most of the other extras from the Gold Box are included, some in extended form. They are scattered throughout the discs. There are a few extras included from the Artisan season one set. As for the extras not on this set, Artisan owns the season one commentaries and didn't license them, so blame Aristan. And the SNL skits and coffee commercials are owned by someone else who also didn't want to license them. I would love to have them all on one set, but that's the way it goes. At least we still have them on the DVD sets. CONCLUSION It is hard to emphasize just how much impact Twin Peaks had on television. It had a short run but its influence is felt to this day. Shows from X-Files to Lost and beyond simply would not have existed without Twin Peaks blazing the trail. The show today still seems fresh and innovative, even though it has spawned 24 years of imitators. If any show deserves the deluxe blu-ray treatment, it is Twin Peaks. So is the set worth the high price tag so many people have been complaining about? Absolutely. The set includes 2 versions of the pilot, 29 hour long episodes and FWWM all newly remastered in HD. Plus you get the 90 minute Missing Pieces newly directed and edited by David Lynch himself in HD, hours of newly produced behind the scenes content and most of the previous extras remastered in HD (some in extended versions). This is far more content than similarly priced HD single season sets (Star Trek and I Love Lucy come to mind). And Twin Peaks is a cult show with a much smaller audience. So the price is more than fair and completely in line with other releases. They could easily have released Season One, Two and FWWM as separate releases which would have cost far more to purchase individually. This set is a dream release for Twin Peaks fans. We never thought we would see the deleted scenes from FWWM, much less finished in beautiful HD quality by Lynch himself. After all those years of watching low quality VHS tapes in the 90s, who would have thought we would get the entire show remastered in HD? If price is a concern, I am sure Amazon will drop the price sometime in the near future. But it is well worth every penny they are charging now.

history.title: Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (4K Restored) [Blu-ray]
history.text: This is a well done restoration with good resolution. However there are numerous scenes where black areas show pixilation and digital tiling. This happens in several instances when the camera irises in/out during a closeup or scene change. It is also visible on the backs of the silhouetted audience during Caligari's show. It can be scene as small clusters of slightly brighter blocks which are constantly moving in the black areas. Some scenes look fine, but there are several with the problem. This is due to compression errors during mastering, not the film itself. Kino mastered the film brighter than it should be, which is part of the problem because it makes these issues more noticeable. The European version of this title uses the same master, but it is darker, so the artifacts are less obvious. Many people won't notice it or will assume it is part of an old movie, but it is really the result of sloppy mastering. It's a shame because it is a nicely done restoration otherwise. Hopefully Kino will release a corrected version with a higher bitrate, which should fix the problem. I will be returning my disc until then.

history.title: Star Trek: The Original Series - The Roddenberry Vault
history.review_title: A mixed bag. Cool footage, but not enough of it and NOT in HD!
history.text: This is a frustrating release. Since it is aimed squarely at the most hardcore fans, I expected better. There is some cool stuff here to be sure, but it could have been so much better with minimal effort. The set contains 12 episodes we all already own many times over, some with new commentaries. 11 of the 12 have isolated scores, which is great. However one of the most popular, City on the Edge of Forever, does not, for no apparent reason. The real attraction is the rare outtakes and deleted footage. It is presented in three 30 minute documentaries and a 20 minute collection of footage spread across 3 discs. The first documentary shows us rows of shelving with hundreds of film cans full of rare, unseen footage. This really serves to whet your appetite. You would think that in 90 minutes of documentary we would get to see a LOT of this footage. But unfortunately the majority of time is spent on people talking about the episodes. In 90 minutes there are MAYBE 10 minutes total of the rare footage that we really want to see. Most of this is shown in short clips, often with people talking over it. It is very, very frustrating. There is no way to just watch the footage without slogging through the documentaries. Add to that the 20 minutes of additional clips on disc 3 (mercifully with no talking heads) and we probably get to see 30 minutes of vault footage in total. On a 3 disc, expensive release, that just doesn't cut it. You can get the entire 3 seasons of the original series in HD for the same price. The footage itself is a treat. However, for reasons I cannot begin to fathom, it is all presented in low quality, standard definition. NONE of the documentaries are in HD, they are all standard definition, even on the blu-ray! This is just plain bizarre. Why would they transfer this rare, valuable footage in standard definition? It makes no sense at all. It's not even much of a cost savings these days. Even though color has faded, the high resolution of the 35mm film is still there and a good HD transfer and very basic color correction would have looked 1000% better than what we get. I'm just mystified as to why it was done this way. And severely disappointed. Paramount has done a pretty terrible, disappointing job with the 50th anniversary. This was the one release which promised to be really exciting. But they botched it. It could have been so much better, and without much additional effort or expense. Use HD transfers, include far more footage and less talking heads. Save the cost of filming the documentaries and invest in HD transfers of the vault footage. Hard core fans would be happy to sit through hours of raw takes, we don't need talking heads to keep us interested. And casual fans aren't going to be interested no matter how it's presented. So cater to your audience. I think we can expect to see several more of these Vault releases in the future (this one only covers 12 episodes). I can only hope they do better if they want my money again.

history.title: Superman The Movie: Extended Cut & Special Edition 2-Film Collection [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: Warner has meticulously transferred the print and done a lot of cleanup to produce a version that looks a hundred times better than the old 1983 version
history.text: Hat's off to Warner Archive for releasing this legendary extended version of Superman the Movie. This version was a true event when it was shown over two nights on ABC in 1983. This was long before the internet or hundreds of cable channels and most people watched what was on the three main networks live. Not only was ABC showing a hugely popular movie, they were showing it with 40 minutes of never before seen footage. This was a mind blowing concept at the time. It was before the era of deleted scenes on DVD and was the first time people were introduced to the concept that scenes were actually cut out of movies. Low quality VHS copies of that ABC version and subsequent 1980s broadcasts have circulated for years among collectors. When WB video released STM in various forms over the years, fans always requested the TV version. Instead, we got the 2000 Special Edition, which restored several of the scenes, but ultimately only 8 of the 40 minutes. It also had a newly remixed soundtrack that replaced many of the familiar sound effects, which turned off many fans from that version. (to clarify, there are 3 versions of STM available: the 143 minute theatrical version, the 151 minute Expanded/Special Edition and the 188 minute Extended TV version. This blu-ray includes the 151 and 188 minute versions). Now here we are in 2017 and Warner Archive has found a holy grail widescreen 35mm print of the TV version miraculously preserved in a vault. Cropped 16mm prints of the TV version have been in the hands of collectors for years, but no one even suspected there was a widescreen 35mm version. Warner has meticulously transferred the print and done a lot of cleanup to produce a version that looks a hundred times better than the old 1983 version, plus reveals 40% more picture because it is in widescreen. It is a bit grainy in places, but that is how film prints from that era look. Many classic films are overly scrubbed of grain, which also removes some fine detail. Considering the age of the print (35+ years) and the fact it was never meant to be seen in high definition, it looks very good and is more detailed than the special edition blu-ray in some places. The audio is mostly in mono, because that is how TV was broadcast back then. Warner did add stereo music to the main and end titles, which leads me to the only negative aspect of this release. They used the wrong version of the main title theme, so it is jarringly and incorrectly edited. I'm sure this was done with good intentions, but they should have just left it as the original mono directly from the TV version, or lifted it from the soundtrack of the theatrical version. Still, this is a minor complaint and won't be noticed by most viewers. It doesn't detract from what is an overall outstanding release. Huge kudos to Warner Archive for releasing this and for doing a fantastic job with it. Highly recommended. I hope they release the unique TV version of Superman II next.

history.title: Twin Peaks: A Limited Event Series [Blu-ray]
history.text: As you can see by the extreme range of reviews, people seem to really love or really hate this series. Is it really the most amazing or the worst thing every created? No. As is usually the case, the truth is somewhere in the middle. It has moments of amazing, surreal brilliance. It also has moments of bad writing, bad acting, indulgence and - the worst thing possible for a David Lynch film - boredom. Spoilers ahead. As others have noted, this is not a continuation of the tone of Twin Peaks the series or the movie Fire Walk With Me. This is a slow moving, extremely dry version of Twin Peaks. much of which has little to do with the town or story lines of Twin Peaks at all. The biggest failure in the opinion of most fans was a lengthy storyline that kept Agent Cooper in Las Vegas as a mindless version of himself who can only parrot back phrases he hears. The characters around him react in a sitcom fashion, seemingly not able to understand that he is basically catatonic. The events are repetitive and have little to do with Twin Peaks or the larger story. The only redeeming aspect of this arduous storyline is the excellent cast. This goes on for a painful 13 out of 18 parts before Cooper is back to himself. We never find out WHY he was in that state, he just wakes up. Then his story quickly branches out into an extremely surreal final 2 parts which are basically impossible to fully understand. Theories abound, but no one has been able to agree on even what the basic plot is, there just isn't enough information. Almost none of the storylines are resolved and it is implied that much, if not all, of the entire Twin Peaks story was a dream. So there is a lot to be justifiably frustrated about for longtime Twin Peaks fans. That said, if you are a David Lynch fan, there is a lot to love. The best parts for me were the crazy, ultra surreal moments. This is Lynch at his experimental best and it's a real mind blasting experience in places. There is just enough of this to keep your interest going during the dreadful Las Vegas scenes and make the series worth watching if you keep your expectations in check. I just wish more of the series had been in that style. So while there is a lot of artistic brilliance and convention defying on display, there are also a lot of flat and sometimes dull moments which move at a glacial pace. The characters are superficial for the most part. We get very little, if any, insight into what Cooper is thinking or feeling or what he is actually doing in the last 2 episodes. The series avoids nostalgia and conventional pacing in some scenes, then turns around and wallows in sitcom level writing and in your face nostalgic references to pie and coffee. It's not the most amazing piece of television ever created (even though some parts reach that level), nor is it the worst piece of crap ever put on screen (even though there are some parts that are a chore to slog through). It is not narratively satisfying, because the narrative is nearly, if not completely, incomprehensible. Only Lynch knows what really happened, and he will never tell. It is a wildly mixed bag across a wide spectrum of styles. It is alternately fascinating and infuriating. Definitely not for everyone, but worth watching for some with proper expectations.

history.title: Moon Machines
history.text: If you're an air and space buff, or anyone with an interest in high tech machines and technological challenges, this is a "must see" video. I watched each segment separately over several days (about an hour each), and although I believe I have a fairly broad depth of knowledge about the space program, I learned a lot and was inspired at the resourceful dedication of all involved in making the Apollo program a success. When you see the history, the multitude of new and seemingly insolvable challenges presented here, it is truly amazing that it all worked, at any price - and on time! Truly America's greatest technological success ever, in my opinion. The Mars missions and nuclear submarines are comparable, but when you consider the mammoth challenges of the Apollo program... Truly amazing. This production presents it clearly, vividly.

history.title: Mars Rising
history.text: I have many space-related documentary type dvds and ordered this one expecting a somewhat shallow, perhaps grade school overview of considerations for a mission to Mars. I was very pleasantly surprised to find a very intelligently written and presented overview of both the technical and human aspects, with exceptional graphics. I was impressed... and motivated. A high quality production overall. Perhaps most interesting to me (& my wife) were the many practical human considerations of lengthy space flight (personalities, sex, boredom, fatigue, friction, health, etc.). Those two segments alone (an hour and a half out of over 5 hours) were worth the purchase price. As a child, I had once thought I'd take a one-way trip to Mars if offered because of the very exciting concept of exploring such an interesting planet. Now I'm not sure that I'd even consider a round trip - extreme dangers (of every imaginable sort), prolonged physical discomfort and a possible loss of one's sanity, to name a few considerations. The reality of today's space exploration is a long, long way from William Shatner's Star Trek. It's conastoga wagon compared to a 757 to cross the continent. Shatner does a fine job of narration, by the way. Bottom line - very informative and entertaining. And, exploring Mars is far more motivating than a similar effort to an asteroid, in my opinion.

history.title: Heist: Who Stole the American Dream?
history.review_title: Too opinionated and not academically rigorous (There's better out there.)
history.text: Based upon other reviews of this DVD, I guess I had much higher expectations for a balanced documentary, or at least a liberal slant that was supported by persuasive facts. I'd be ok with that bias, if I were expecting it, although I'd much prefer a balanced presentation of interviews and facts without an obvious political agenda (liberal or conservative). I can make up my own mind if I'm presented a clear argument and all of the pertinent facts. The critique of Ronald Reagan's showdown with the federally employed air traffic controllers union was a very poor choice as an example in support of unions, for example. To most people (pro union or not), the ATC union strike was an obvious public safety and freedom of commerce issue, and a bad example of an arrogant, self centered union gone amuck. If you want a liberal slant, a much more persuasive and academically rigorous one is provided by Robert Reich (a UC Berkley professor, former U.S. Secretary of Labor) in the documentary, "Inequality for All". It had self-deprecating humor, interesting & relevant facts and never insulted my intelligence. The resulting presentation br Reich, in contrast, was much more persuasive in supporting a similar ideological conclusion.

history.title: Inequality For All
history.review_title: Can't argue with the facts. Well done!
history.text: Humorous, educational, doesn't insult your intelligence. I have a much better opinion of UC Berkley, if Robert Reich is on staff there. My conservative friends will think I've defected, but you can't argue with a cogently presented documentary. It may not give the whole story, but what it does, it does well. I say, give the public (those who care anyway) the honest facts from all sides of an argument and assume we have the intelligence to make up our own minds. This documentary is a good step in the right direction, regardless of your political persuasion.

Excellent graphics and production values. Highly recommended!

history.text: Depressing film. It is a about a woman who has child after child with an alcoholic husband prone to raging and violent, destructive outbursts. I think it was terribly sad that not only was SHE in denial about her husband and made excuse after excuse for him? She subjected her children to decades of walking about on eggshells and having no choice but to live in such an environment themselves. I didn't view her as strong; I viewed her as weak. She proved time and again how very capable she was, in providing for the family as her husband wasn't able to, so she could have taken her children and left that environment. She could have given them a chance at a happy, loving home. The true theme was quite dark really, and not at all what I was expecting, so I wasn't pleased. The children are more background than anything really, and you certainly don't get to know them (except for one daughter)...and we are barely even made aware of their names. At the end of the film though, they provide an update on those children's futures: how they grew up and are living their lives now. I thought that was a bit odd, as you hadn't the chance to invest anything in these characters at all. Be aware this is not a light hearted, fun family film at all.

history.title: CINDERELLA
history.text: I had resisted seeing this for so long, but found myself quite pleasantly surprised by it. It had real heart and beauty, and I found myself quite touched, and in tears here and there. The characters had depth, and weren't over the top, as I expected. The wicked stepsisters weren't all that wicked, and I even felt empathy for the stepmother at different times. It was lovely, and an exceptional retelling of the classic tale.

I don't get all the hype. I even watched it a second time, thinking perhaps I didn't give it a fair chance initially. Turns out I did. I liked Tangled MUCH better, and it didn't get near the attention, though it was quite deserving of it.

**MAJOR SPOILER ALERT** I thought this series was very very well done, but I truly had 'the killer' picked out early on. There was no logical reason for them to continually show the inn keeper in the background. He never had any lines or place in the narrative, outside of 'foretelling'. I will also say I was displeased with how it ended. I felt it would be picked up in Season 2, so imagine my displeasure at finding out Season 2 would be an entirely new story! So...there will never be an answer!

I attempted to watch this, twice, but couldn't make it through. It comes down to being extremely attached to and fond of the original; I admit to being unable to give the new version a chance. Visually, it is stunning; it just doesn't have the heart of the original. The way they have drastically switched up the characters is disconcerting as well. One example is Kaa being a female. Kaa in the original, so perfectly voiced by Sterling Holloway, has no equal as it is. Switching 'him' to a female?? WHY??? There are certain original films that are so completely perfect, just the way they are, there should be a law against 're-making' them. The Little Mermaid, E.T., The Wizard of Oz, all of The Toy Story films, and certainly The Jungle Book.

history.text: The first disk,"Sharpe's Justice", takes place in the time between "Sharpe's Revenge" and "Waterloo" not covered by the Cornwell novels. It is an interesting story using Sharpe's early life in an orphans workhouse, the bitterness between him and his wife and her lover, and several characters from previous stories to make a fine tale. Although there is less action and more conniving than in previous episodes and the enemies are Sharpe's own countrymen instead of the French, I feel it fits well into the Sharpe series. The second disk, "Sharpe's Waterloo", is an excellent adaption of the book considering the vastness of the story's scope, although for those who haven't read the book Jane's fate will not be quite so fitting. The third disk, "Sharpe The Legend" is only a bit of fluff, but not so offensive as some viewers seem to feel. (and you can use it as bait to get your friends hooked on the series)

history.review_title: Death Wish 6 or 7? by Asghar Farhadi
history.text: I don't know what number Charles Bronson left off at in that series, and who would have expected the best auteur in the world to pick up where he left off, but here we are. It just goes to show what a hundred-monkey operation the Academy is that they would give this film any kind of a nod. This is not what we were hoping for next from the director of A Separation and The Past but hopefully he'll raise the bar again next time instead of limboing low again. You can tell by the difference in time the director took in the bonus material what he thinks of his achievement here. Just a 15 minute interview says all there is to say about this one. You can see the craft of a great filmmaker at work here, but it's basically a misfire and all we have is just an ugly little revenge film that I would rather not have seen. I liked the scenes with the little boy the best. I wish he was in a better movie!

history.title: The Daughter
history.text: This is actually a four star movie that only drops to a 3 star because of the pull the rug out ending, but it is still a movie NOT TO BE MISSED that is way better than most of the garbage out there. In actual movie reviews, 3 stars is very solid and 4 stars is cream of the crop, 5 stars is once in a blue moon. But most Amazon reviews are 5 star/1 star. I'm giving it 5 Amazon stars here to pull it back up from the wrong-headed reviews some of the other Amazon reviewers have posted. This is quality stuff. I was thoroughly engaged throughout and although I didn't like the ending, I expect I'll like it better than Ibsen's original ending. Or if it's the same in the play then I'll have to forgive the filmmakers for just staying true to the source. I definitely plan to listen to the play now (The Wild Duck by Henrik Ibsen, available free from Librivox.org, or 6 bucks from Audible.) I was very pleasantly surprised by this movie because I went into it with no expectations really. Very nice acting, complicated performances, organic adaptation of a play from 1884 to contemporary times.

history.title: Song to Song
history.text: Please ignore the idiotic characterization by Amazon that this is an "HD-DVD that will only play in HD-DVD players". Of course it's a UHD Blu and you need that kind of a player. Now, my review: This is for Terrence Malick fans only, a difficult movie for anyone else. And, if you're like me, you're thinking "At last! A real art-house movie on UHD Blu!" But beware that it's not HDR, just 4K, so the video quality doesn't compare with other UHD Blus out there. So we're still waiting.... (Criterion?! Helloo?) This movie took about 38 minutes to get me, at first it just looks like a mess. That's Malick the auteur beating us over the head and demanding complete submission. The movie looks at first like a bunch of amateurish disconnected rubbish. But it later coalesces into a kind of found-footage movie with a nice love-story at the heart of it instead of a horror movie. Instead of a kid with a camcorder accidentally documenting everything you have a mad auteur, more concerned with herky jerky hand-held camera, flocks of birds, weird fish-eye lens shots etc. And yet somehow a very solid story begins to build from these "accidental" elements. And the nice Malickian nuances begin to support the emerging narrative. Great performance from Rooney Mara. At the end I wanted to watch it again and I bet the first half-hour would have made more sense.

history.title: Right Now Wrong Then

There was no reason for this and nothing to be gained from this experiment. It was like a rerun of a film you would never watch twice otherwise, without any chance to forget the first viewing in between. I really started to squirm in my chair when I realized what was happening but it was too late to start watching anything else. Skip this.
I guess this movie isn't any good or there would be a Blu-ray.

history.title: Spin Out
history.text: Spin Out is about racing with cars in the Australian Outback in an attempt to outmaneuver each other by spinning round and round until one is declared the winner in a kind of "game of chicken". It really isn't that clear. But that's only the backdrop for a film that moves at a snail's pace towards finding true love and reconciling one's feelings that seem to have been submerged forever. The box for the disc proudly proclaims: "An affectionate fusion of Project X and Love Actually". Actually, it's more like Animal House meets The Dukes of Hazzard. Trite and predictable don't begin to define this movie which plods along to its inevitable end. All the standard jokes and gross outs are there - from a portable worker's outhouse that explodes with someone in there resulting in..., grown men dressing in drag, binge drinking contests, mud wrestling, nude flashing, etc. The only bright spot is to see the incomparable Xavier Samuel (Twilight, Adore, Bait, Drift, Anonymous, Newcastle) who must have had some free time on his hands to make this film and earn a few extra bucks. It does not help his career. The idea for this movie must have looked better on paper than in the final outcome. The last extended scene in the film reminds one of that found in Grease without the great music, production values, and dancing that we see in the latter. Ironically, it is Olivia Newton John, an Australian, who is one of the two major stars of Grease and is responsible for setting up the entire finale of that film. Maybe they should have borrowed her to make a cameo appearance in this one. Forget Spin Out. It will only make your head spin!

history.title: Kong: Skull Island
history.text: Theatre Review: This film is far more than a mere reboot or remake. I saw it in 3-D and I as well as the people around me were jumping and flinching throughout the movie as object after object came zooming out at us. The film has a solid script, fine acting, and CGI effects the likes of which stand at the very pinnacle of this genre. This may be the most credible and "three dimensional" Kong ever presented from the standpoint of his size, strength, actions, behavior, and appearance. While the story does follow several tried and true as well as predictable paths, the way that many of the would be hunters are dispatched is brought to a new level of gore and, combined with the intensity of this film, is not for the squeamish.The movie begins with same kind of rationale that was seen at the beginning of the Godzilla reboot for the South Pacific atomic testing of the early 1950s. But, from then on nothing is like the latter. Indeed, Kong makes a very early appearance and one need not wait until you are 60% or more into this film for it to happen. The setting on Skull Island is far superior to the California civic setting of Godzilla and far deadlier and forbidding. Kong's creature opponents alone make this film more sinister and exciting - and help to elevate the special effects to a whole new level. The balance between Kong's "humanity" and his "monster side" is perfectly done. While Samuel L. Jackson's character does tend to chew up the scenery he is necessary as the usual human foil for Kong. As a deranged soldier who, in 1973 (the chronological setting for this film), still cannot accept the end result in Vietnam, Jackson's attitude and emotional posturing make Kong appear that much more human. One disappointment was the way the "WALL" on Skull Island was introduced and the reason given for it even though it was intended to fit the storyline of this particular Kong. In the end, it was basically a mere homage to previous Kong movies and something of a throw away. For those who have never seen it, this Kong movie was far more reminiscent of a 1948 film titled "Unknown Island" with Richard Denning, Virginia Grey, and Barton MacLane. That film even had a most threatening oversized prehistoric sloth which even does battle with a T-Rex near the end. (A DVD of the film is still available on Amazon.) Another surprise for me is the fact that Kong: Skull Island is not doing as well by some $30million so far in the US and Canada compared to Godzilla even though IMHO the former is a much better film in every way. However, overseas business is very brisk so far and should well exceed Godzilla when the final tally is made. A final note: For anyone who has yet to see Kong be sure and wait till the end of all the end credits. People always leave the theatre as soon as the credits begin to roll. I don't. And a key Epilogue scene was missed. Serves them right.

history.title: The Great Epochs of European Art: Early Christian and Byzantine Art, Romanesque Art & Gothic Art
history.review_title: A GOOD VISUAL INTRODUCTION FOR STUDENTS AND LAYMEN ALIKE
history.text: Despite the broad range of its coverage (some 1000 years of Eastern and Western Christian art), I found the section on Byzantium in this DVD to be quite helpful for my students in a course on The Art of Byzantium & Russia. In itself, it is not the be all and end all but does complement the basic textbook(s) that were being used. The neglect that is given to the art and architecture of the above mentioned two cultures makes any available visual material especially worthwhile. Just glance at the listings in art history for any number of universities and colleges around the country to see what I mean. The importance of Russia and contemporary Istanbul (formerly Constantinople) in the present world absolutely demands more material on Byzantium and its heir - Russia. There is a more comprehensive approach in John Romer's "Byzantium: The Lost Empire" that comes in a 2 DVD set and is also available from Amazon. However, his approach is a bit heavy and a bit breathless in its subjectivity and, at times, rambling nature. Nevertheless, for the inquisitive layman and student alike who have any interest or curiosity regarding Byzantium (a modern appellation applied to the Christianized Eastern Roman Empire that survived its Western counterpart by nearly 1000 years) and its art, this is highly recommended.
